course.title: Western Philosophy: A Guided Reading Course
course.subtitle: What to read next, from the Pre-Socratics to now
course.description: A professor-designed sequence of exact sittings: the pages that teach the move, why they come now, what to look for, and the questions that make the next text possible. Primary texts are the course. Public-domain English translations are hosted in the app; in-copyright works are assigned as bibliographic readings you obtain legally.
course.audience: Self-taught student; no prior philosophy required
course.method:
Read in order. Home always names the next unread assignment; do not skip ahead to the famous title. Each sitting is 20–90 minutes unless the text itself refuses to be cut. Read the assigned pages, not the surrounding commentary, unless the assignment is marked secondary.

Keep a notebook. For every sitting, write (1) the claim in one or two sentences without jargon, (2) the best objection you can find in the text or invent honestly, and (3) one question you could not settle. Those three lines are the course’s memory.

When a reading is hosted in the app, read it there. The outbound URL is the bibliographic record and a backup. When an assignment is bibliographic, get a library or purchased copy. Do not use a pirated scan. Later units assume earlier ones: Hume will not make sense if you have only a rumor of Descartes; Kant will not make sense if Hume is a rumor; the twentieth century will not make sense if Kant is a rumor.

You are not collecting opinions. You are learning a set of moves — how a question is posed, how an argument is forced, and how a later writer inherits a problem. If a sitting feels too short, reread it. If it feels too long, slow down; the split assignments exist so you never have to swallow a system in one evening.

After each sitting, take the quiz. It is not a trap; it is the seminar’s check that you caught the move. Missed items point you back into the pages, not to a summary.

eras.title: The Pre-Socratics
eras.intro: Philosophy begins when the world is asked to explain itself without being a story about the gods’ moods. The Milesians look for an underlying stuff and a process; Heraclitus and Parmenides then force a crisis: if everything changes, what can be known, and if what is cannot not-be, how can there be change at all? You are not collecting slogans about water or fire. You are watching the first disciplined fight over nature, logos, and being — the fight Plato and Aristotle inherit.

units.title: From myth to nature
units.professorNote: Start with a short orientation, then the Milesians. Burnet is dated, and that is useful: you see an older reconstruction of fragments rather than a modern handbook’s smoothness. Read him for the fragments and the problem, not for every conjecture.

assignments.title: Why these fragments matter
assignments.author: John Burnet
assignments.pages: Burnet, Introduction (through the discussion of ‘nature’ and coming-to-be)
assignments.why: You cannot meet Heraclitus or Parmenides as isolated aphorists. Burnet’s opening shows why the first philosophers are doing something different from myth even when they still talk of gods, and why ‘nothing comes from nothing’ is already a constraint on explanation. Read this so the fragments later feel like arguments, not tattoos.
lookFor: What counts, for Burnet, as the break from mythological explanation
The principle that nothing comes to be from nothing — and why it will haunt the next units
How ‘nature’ (physis) is being used as a name for what underlies change
questions: In one sentence, what is the Milesian project if it is not ‘science’ in our sense?
Why would a constraint on coming-to-be force a crisis about change?
assignments.nextHint: Next you meet the first answers: water, the indefinite, air.

quiz.title: After Burnet’s introduction
quiz.intro: Check that you caught why these fragments are arguments, not mottos.

questions.prompt: For Burnet, a leading constraint already at work among the early cosmologists is that

options.text: the gods created the world from a prior chaos of stories
nothing comes into being out of nothing, and nothing passes into nothing
all change is illusion generated by the senses
nature is whatever the poets already named

questions.explanation: Burnet treats ‘nothing from nothing’ as the principle that will make change itself a problem — the hinge toward Parmenides.

questions.prompt: In this introduction, ‘nature’ (physis) is most usefully heard as

options.text: the national character of the Greeks
a name for the underlying stuff and process of the world, as opposed to mere tale
the moral law written in the heart
whatever biology will later mean by ‘species’

questions.explanation: The point of the sitting is the break from mythological explanation toward an account of what underlies coming-to-be.

questions.prompt: Burnet wants you to treat Thales’ ‘water’ as a modern chemical hypothesis.
questions.explanation: He is reconstructing a first attempt to name an underlying nature, not a lab result. Reading it as chemistry misses the philosophical move.

assignments.title: Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes
assignments.author: John Burnet
assignments.translator: Burnet’s English of the fragments and testimonies
assignments.selection: The Milesian School — Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter I (skip later scholarly disputes once you have the three positions)
assignments.why: Three attempts to name what the world is ‘from.’ Thales’ water is less interesting as meteorology than as the claim that diverse things share an underlying nature. Anaximander’s apeiron and the language of justice between opposites is the first hint that explanation may need something not itself a familiar element. Anaximenes’ air and condensation is a process-story: difference is rarefaction and compression. Get these three on the table before flux and being.
lookFor: Whether ‘water’ is an element in our sense or a stand-in for the living, the moist, the source
Anaximander’s apeiron: why the origin cannot be one of the opposites it explains
Anaximenes: a mechanism (rarefaction/condensation) rather than a mere name of stuff
questions: Which Milesian is doing cosmology, and which is already doing a kind of metaphysics?
If you had to defend one of the three as the most philosophically ambitious, which and why?
assignments.nextHint: Xenophanes will attack the gods of the poets; then Heraclitus will refuse a stable stuff altogether.

quiz.title: After the Milesians
quiz.intro: Three first answers: stuff, the indefinite, and a process.

questions.prompt: Anaximander’s apeiron is philosophically ambitious because it

options.text: identifies the origin with ordinary water, which we can see
treats the origin as not itself one of the opposed elements it would have to explain
is simply the Greek word for Zeus

questions.explanation: If the origin were one of the opposites (hot, cold, wet), it could not fairly explain the rest. The indefinite is a step toward a principle that is not a familiar body.

questions.prompt: Anaximenes’ distinctive contribution in Burnet’s chapter is mainly

options.text: a moral theory of justice among cities
rarefaction and condensation as a mechanism of difference
the claim that void is the only reality

questions.explanation: Air becomes other things by being thinned or packed — a process-story, not only a new name of stuff.

questions.prompt: Thales’ water is most interesting, in this course’s terms, as

options.text: the claim that diverse things share an underlying nature
a proof that the gods do not exist

questions.explanation: The sitting asked you to hear a metaphysical decision: one nature of many things — not a weather report.

units.title: Logos, critique of the poets, flux
units.professorNote: Xenophanes shows that theology can be criticized. Heraclitus shows that order might live inside change. Read the fragments slowly; do not let ‘flux’ become a slogan.

assignments.title: Xenophanes against the poets
assignments.author: Xenophanes
assignments.selection: The Xenophanes pages in ‘Science and Religion’
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter II, Xenophanes of Kolophon (the fragments on the gods and on one greatest god)
assignments.why: Before Socrates, someone already says: the poets attribute to the gods theft, adultery, and whatever is a shame among men; and that mortals make gods in their own image. This is not atheism as a modern identity. It is the claim that a serious account of the divine cannot be a projection of our vices and our local shapes. You need this before you hear Socrates on piety.
lookFor: The ethnological jab: Ethiopians’ gods, Thracians’ gods
What ‘one god, greatest among gods and men’ does and does not settle
Whether this is theology, epistemology, or cultural criticism — or all three
questions: Is Xenophanes replacing myth with a better story, or refusing story-form?
What would a Xenophanean critique of a modern ‘god of the gaps’ look like?
assignments.nextHint: Heraclitus will keep the divine in the account — as logos and fire — without letting it be a character in a poem.

quiz.title: After Xenophanes
quiz.intro: Theology can be criticized. That is the move.

questions.prompt: Xenophanes’ ethnological jab (Ethiopians’, Thracians’ gods) is meant to suggest that

options.text: all peoples have already reached the same true theology
mortals fashion gods in their own image
only Greeks should be allowed to speak of the divine
the gods have no interest in human shape at all, so the jab is irrelevant

questions.explanation: The fragments treat local gods as projections. That is a critique of the poets’ theology, not a travelogue.

questions.prompt: The ‘one god, greatest among gods and men’ fragment

options.text: settles the whole later problem of divine attributes
criticizes anthropomorphic religion without yet being a full natural theology
proves that the Milesians were secretly priests

questions.explanation: Xenophanes attacks shameful stories and local shapes; he does not hand you Aquinas. Do not over-read.

questions.prompt: Xenophanes is best read as replacing myth with a better story of the same kind.
questions.explanation: The sitting asked whether he replaces story-form or refuses it. The fragments strain against the poets’ narrative gods.

assignments.title: Heraclitus: logos, strife, the river
assignments.author: Heraclitus
assignments.work: Fragments, in Early Greek Philosophy, ch. III
assignments.selection: Selected fragments: B1, B2, B12, B50, B51, B80, B123, and the surrounding Burnet discussion
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter III, especially the fragments on logos, war, and the river
assignments.why: Heraclitus is the first writer in this course who will punish you for paraphrase. The logos is common, but people live as if they had a private understanding. Strife is not a regrettable accident; it is how things hold together. The river fragments do not say ‘nothing is stable’ in the lazy sense — they ask how something can be the same while it flows. Read until you can state the view without the word ‘flux.’
lookFor: What ‘logos’ seems to mean in B1–B2 — speech, measure, account, the way things are
Whether the river fragments imply no stability, or a stability that is the pattern of change
War/strife as justice (B80) versus a mere celebration of violence
questions: Can you state Heraclitus’s view without the word ‘flux’?
If the logos is common, why does he sound so contemptuous of ‘the many’?
assignments.nextHint: Parmenides will deny the road of not-being. Keep Heraclitus’s river in mind as the view being refused.

quiz.title: After Heraclitus
quiz.intro: State the view without the word ‘flux.’

questions.prompt: In the fragments Burnet gathers, logos is most nearly

options.text: a private opinion each person is entitled to
the common account or measure of how things are, which people miss by living as if they had a private understanding
a later Stoic technical term Heraclitus could not have meant

questions.explanation: B1–B2: the logos is common; people live as though they had a private understanding. That is the teaching, not a later textbook definition.

questions.prompt: The river fragments are most carefully read as

options.text: proof that nothing is identical for even an instant, so names are useless
a question about how something can be the same while it flows — order inside change

questions.explanation: The sitting warned against the lazy slogan ‘nothing is stable.’ The philosophical pressure is identity-through-change.

questions.prompt: Strife (war) in these fragments is

options.text: a regrettable accident to be eliminated by a future justice
presented as how things hold together — even as justice
only a metaphor for civil war in Ephesus

questions.explanation: B80 and related fragments make conflict constitutive, not a glitch. That is why ‘flux’ as chaos is the wrong paraphrase.

questions.prompt: You can state Heraclitus’s view adequately with only the word ‘flux.’
questions.explanation: The assignment’s own question: logos, measure, and strife drop out if you only say ‘everything changes.’

units.title: Being and the Eleatic challenge
units.professorNote: This is the hinge of early Greek philosophy. If Parmenides is right, cosmology as the Milesians did it is a mistake. Plato’s forms and Aristotle’s potentiality are, in part, replies.

assignments.title: Parmenides: the way of truth
assignments.author: Parmenides
assignments.selection: The Way of Truth (and Burnet’s brief frame); glance at the Way of Opinion so you see the contrast
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter IV, especially the Way of Truth fragments
assignments.why: Parmenides tells you there are two roads: that it is, and that it is not. The second cannot be thought or said. From that he unpacks: what is is ungenerated, imperishable, whole, unmoving. This is not poetry about a sphere for its own sake. It is a ban on explaining what is by what is not — coming-to-be, difference, and empty space all come under suspicion. If you feel the room tilt, the course is working.
lookFor: The two roads, and why ‘is not’ cannot be a way of inquiry
What follows for coming-to-be and perishing
The ‘sphere’ language: metaphor, cosmology, or a claim about completeness
questions: Does Parmenides deny change, or deny that change can be thought as a passage through not-being?
What would a Milesian have to give up if this argument holds?
assignments.nextHint: Zeno will defend this with paradoxes you already half-know. Then pluralists will try to save the appearances.

quiz.title: After Parmenides’ way of truth
quiz.intro: If what is cannot not-be, cosmology as the Milesians did it is in trouble.

questions.prompt: The two roads in the Way of Truth are, most nearly,

options.text: that it is, and that it is not — and the second cannot be a way of inquiry

questions.explanation: You cannot think or say what is not. That ban is the argument, not a travel metaphor.

questions.prompt: From the ban on not-being, Parmenides unpacks that what is is

options.text: endlessly generated and destroyed, like the river
ungenerated, imperishable, and not genuinely many in the way mortals say
only a useful fiction of the city

questions.explanation: Coming-to-be would be a passage through not-being. That is why change and plurality come under suspicion.

questions.prompt: The ‘sphere’ language is best treated, at this stage of the course, as

options.text: a proof that the earth is round
a claim about completeness and lack of deficiency, whether or not it is also cosmology
a joke at Homer’s expense only

questions.explanation: Do not reduce it to astronomy. Completeness is the metaphysical point Burnet’s sitting asked you to hear.

assignments.title: Zeno’s paradoxes of motion
assignments.author: Zeno of Elea
assignments.selection: The younger Eleatics — Zeno on plurality and motion
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter VIII, Zeno (Achilles, the arrow, dichotomy — as Burnet reconstructs them)
assignments.why: Zeno is not a puzzle-book. He is Parmenides’ bodyguard: if you insist on many things and on motion, you inherit contradictions. Read the paradoxes as pressure on the idea that space and time are infinitely divisible, and on the idea that a thing is a sum of parts. Aristotle will spend a career answering this; you only need to feel why an answer is required.
lookFor: Whether the target is motion as such, or a certain picture of space/time as points
The difference between ‘never finishes the halves’ and ‘the arrow is at rest in an instant’
How plurality (many things) is as threatened as locomotion
questions: If you had to pick one paradox as philosophically deepest, which, and what assumption does it attack?
Is Zeno proving Parmenides, or only refuting the opponents’ physics?
assignments.nextHint: Empedocles, Anaxagoras, and the atomists will try to keep being from not-being without denying the world of change.

quiz.title: After Zeno
quiz.intro: Paradoxes as bodyguard, not puzzle-book.

questions.prompt: Zeno’s paradoxes of motion, in Burnet’s reconstruction, are primarily

options.text: pressure on a certain picture of plurality and of infinitely divisible space and time, in defense of Parmenides
proofs that athletes should not race

questions.explanation: He is Parmenides’ bodyguard: if you keep many things and motion, you inherit contradictions.

questions.prompt: The arrow paradox, as a philosophical attack, targets

options.text: the idea that at an instant the flying arrow occupies a place equal to itself — and so seems at rest
the existence of time altogether, in Augustine’s later sense

questions.explanation: If ‘being at a place’ at an instant is indistinguishable from rest, motion as a sum of instants is in trouble.

questions.prompt: Zeno’s aim in this chapter is mainly to invent a new positive cosmology.
questions.explanation: The younger Eleatics are defensive and refutative. Positive cosmology after Parmenides waits for the pluralists and atomists.

units.title: Saving the appearances
units.professorNote: After Parmenides, cosmology has to be a theory of mixture, seeds, or atoms — rearrangement, not generation from nothing. These pages exist so Plato’s ‘participation’ and Aristotle’s ‘potentiality’ do not look like unmotivated jargon.

assignments.title: Mixture, Love and Strife, Mind
assignments.author: Empedocles and Anaxagoras
assignments.selection: Empedocles’ four roots and two forces; Anaxagoras on seeds and Nous — Burnet’s fragment selections, not every testimony
assignments.pages: Burnet, Chapter V (the cosmic cycle and the four roots) and Chapter VI (Nous; ‘in everything a portion of everything’)
assignments.why: Empedocles keeps Parmenides’ ban on genuine coming-to-be: what we call birth is mixture of ungenerated roots, driven by Love and Strife. Anaxagoras keeps mixture too, but makes Mind the arranger — a first hint that explanation may require intelligence, not only stuff. You are watching the invention of a strategy: save change by making it rearrangement.
lookFor: How ‘birth’ is rewritten as mixture so that nothing comes from nothing
Love and Strife as causes versus as mythic names
Anaxagoras’s Nous: why mind is introduced, and whether it actually does any work in the fragments
questions: Is rearrangement enough to explain qualitative difference (life, thought, color)?
Socrates in the Phaedo will complain that Anaxagoras promised mind and delivered airs and aethers. On this reading, is the complaint fair?
assignments.nextHint: The atomists give the most economical version of the same strategy: atoms and void.

quiz.title: After mixture and Mind
quiz.intro: Save change by making it rearrangement.

questions.prompt: Empedocles’ strategy for honoring Parmenides while saving the world of change is to treat ‘birth’ as

options.text: mixture and separation of ungenerated roots

questions.explanation: Nothing genuine comes to be; what we call birth is rearrangement of the four roots under Love and Strife.

questions.prompt: Anaxagoras introduces Nous (Mind) because

options.text: he wants a first hint that arrangement may require intelligence, not only stuff
he denies that anything is mixed
he thinks void explains all order

questions.explanation: The sitting: Mind as arranger. Socrates’ later complaint in the Phaedo is that the promise of Mind is not paid in mechanical details — which you were asked to weigh.

questions.prompt: Love and Strife in Empedocles function most nearly as

options.text: two more chemical elements beside the four roots
moving causes of mixture and separation — whether or not they still wear mythic names

questions.explanation: They are the dynamics of the cycle, not extra stuff of the same type as earth or fire.

assignments.title: Atoms and void
assignments.author: Leucippus and Democritus
assignments.selection: Leukippos/Democritus: atoms, void, and the denial of genuine coming-to-be
assignments.why: Void is the Eleatic scandal made productive: ‘what is not’ is allowed as empty place so that atoms can move. Atoms themselves are Parmenidean little beings — uncuttable, ungenerated — and the world is their collisions. This is the ancestor of every later materialism you will meet, from Lucretius to Hobbes. Read it as a philosophical decision, not as a lucky guess about chemistry.
lookFor: Why void is required if atoms are to move
How atomic differences (shape, arrangement) are supposed to explain sensible qualities
What happens to mind, value, and the gods on this picture
questions: Is the void ‘what is not,’ and if so has Parmenides been answered or ignored?
What would you still not understand about a living animal if you had a complete atomic inventory?
assignments.nextHint: You now have the problem-space Socrates walks into: nature-explanations that do not yet tell you how to live.

quiz.title: After atoms and void
quiz.intro: The Eleatic scandal made productive.

questions.prompt: On the atomist picture Burnet presents, void is required because

options.text: atoms cannot move or rearrange if there is no empty place

questions.explanation: Uncuttable beings need somewhere to go. Void is ‘what is not’ put to work — the Eleatic scandal made into a physics.

questions.prompt: Atoms themselves are, philosophically,

options.text: Parmenidean little beings: ungenerated, uncuttable, differing by shape and arrangement
only a manner of speaking about qualities

questions.explanation: The sitting: rearrangement, not generation from nothing — with a plurality of beings Parmenides would not have allowed.

questions.prompt: If you had a complete atomic inventory of an animal, the atomists think you would automatically understand life and thought.
questions.explanation: The assignment asked what you would still not understand. Qualities, mind, and value are exactly the leftover problem this picture bequeaths.

eras.title: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle
eras.intro: Socrates makes philosophy a way of testing a life in public. Plato writes that testing as drama, then builds a metaphysics of Forms to explain how we can know and how a city can be just. Aristotle refuses to let the Forms do that work from outside the world: substance, nature, and happiness have to be understood in things and in activity. By the end of this era you should be able to state what a Socratic question is, what the Cave is for, and what Aristotle means by eudaimonia and virtue — not as slogans.

units.title: The Socratic test
units.professorNote: Three short dialogues. Euthyphro is the method; Apology is the life; Crito is the political cost. Do not skip Euthyphro because it is about ‘piety’ — it is about definition.

assignments.title: Euthyphro: piety and definition
assignments.author: Plato (Socrates as speaker)
assignments.why: Euthyphro is sure he knows what piety is because he is prosecuting his father. Socrates asks for the form — the one thing by which pious acts are pious — and every answer either names an example, or collapses into a circle (loved by the gods because pious, or pious because loved). This is the Socratic move you will need for the rest of the course: a definition that can survive ‘why?’. The famous fork — is it pious because the gods love it, or do they love it because it is pious? — is the ancestor of every later fight about whether value is will or intellect.
lookFor: The demand for a single form, not a list of pious actions
The Euthyphro dilemma and which horn Euthyphro actually occupies
How the dialogue ends: aporia as a result, not an accident
questions: Why isn’t ‘what the gods love’ a definition even if it happens to be true of all pious things?
Does Socrates know what piety is, or only how to show that Euthyphro doesn’t?
assignments.nextHint: Apology will show what this habit of questioning looks like when a city puts it on trial.

quiz.title: After Euthyphro
quiz.intro: Definition that can survive ‘why?’

questions.prompt: Socrates’ demand that Euthyphro state ‘the form’ of piety is a demand for

options.text: a long list of pious actions
the one character by which pious things are pious — a definition, not an example

questions.explanation: Lists and cases fail because they do not say what piety is. That is the Socratic move the sitting named.

questions.prompt: The Euthyphro dilemma asks, in effect, whether the gods love the pious because it is pious, or

options.text: whether Zeus is stronger than Cronus
whether it is pious merely because the gods love it
whether piety is a craft like horsemanship only

questions.explanation: If piety is only ‘what the gods love,’ the gods’ love looks arbitrary; if they love it because it is pious, piety is independent of their love. Euthyphro cannot hold both.

questions.prompt: The dialogue ends in aporia because

options.text: every offered definition collapses, and that failure is the lesson

questions.explanation: Aporia is the result, not an accident. You were asked whether Socrates knows piety or only how to show that Euthyphro does not.

questions.prompt: ‘What the gods love’ would be a successful definition if it happened to be true of all pious things.
questions.explanation: Even a true coincidence of extension is not the form — the ‘why’ that makes pious things pious.

assignments.title: Apology: philosophy on trial
assignments.author: Plato (Socrates as speaker)
assignments.why: Read this as a public argument about what a life of examination is worth. The oracle story is not autobiography for its own sake: it frames ignorance as a discipline. Notice how Socrates distinguishes his old accusers (the comic reputation) from the formal charges, and how he refuses to beg. The unexamined life line is cheap if you quote it; expensive if you ask what examination costs a city and a family. Jowett is imperfect, but he is public domain and readable. Keep the Stephanus numbers in mind if you later compare a better translation.
lookFor: What Socrates says he does not know — and what he claims to know about death and duty
The oracle, the cross-examination of politicians, poets, and craftsmen
Why he will not stop philosophizing even to save his life
questions: Is the claim of ignorance a method, a pose, or a moral stance?
What would it mean for a city to take his offer of a ‘penalty’ (free meals) seriously?
assignments.nextHint: Crito asks whether the man who defied the jury should defy the laws by escaping.

quiz.title: After the Apology
quiz.intro: Philosophy as a public life, not a hobby.

questions.prompt: The oracle story is in the speech primarily to

options.text: frame Socratic ignorance as a task: testing those who claim wisdom
show that Socrates is the wisest because he knows chemistry
entertain the jury with Delphi tourism

questions.explanation: Ignorance is a discipline. The oracle is the dramatic premise of the examinations of politicians, poets, and craftsmen.

questions.prompt: Socrates refuses to stop philosophizing because

options.text: he enjoys irritating powerful men for its own sake
he treats the examined life as a duty he will not trade for acquittal
the law explicitly requires daily debate in the agora
he expects to be paid a salary by the Thirty

questions.explanation: The sitting: the unexamined life line is expensive. He will not beg and will not quit the practice that produced the charges.

questions.prompt: When Socrates claims not to know, he is best heard as

options.text: confessing total skepticism about everything including duty
a method and moral stance: he knows he lacks the wisdom others pretend to

questions.explanation: He still claims things about death, duty, and the god. Ignorance is not a pose that nothing matters.

questions.prompt: The ‘old accusers’ (comic reputation) and the formal charges are the same group of men.
questions.explanation: He distinguishes the long-standing prejudice from Meletus’s indictment. Mixing them is a common misreading.

assignments.title: Crito: the laws and the just man
assignments.author: Plato (Socrates as speaker)
assignments.why: Crito has money, friends, and a plan. Socrates answers with a personification of the Laws: you were free to leave; you stayed; escape would destroy the legal order you have used. Whether or not you accept that argument, you now have an early social-contract claim on the table — and a severe thesis: one must not return injustice for injustice. Read it against Apology. The same man who will not flatter a jury will not injure the city to save his skin.
lookFor: The principle: never do injustice, even in return
The Laws’ speech: agreement, gratitude, persuasion-or-obedience
What counts as ‘destroying the laws’ by a single escape
questions: Does the Laws’ speech assume a consent Socrates never actually gave?
Can the Apology’s defiance of the jury be made consistent with Crito’s obedience to the laws?
assignments.nextHint: Meno turns the method on virtue and knowledge — and introduces recollection.

quiz.title: After Crito
quiz.intro: The man who defied a jury will not injure the laws to save his skin.

questions.prompt: The Laws’ speech claims Socrates would do wrong to escape because

options.text: he has lived under and used the city’s laws and may not destroy them by private violence

questions.explanation: Persuade-or-obey, gratitude, agreement by remaining: that is the early contract claim, whether or not you accept it.

questions.prompt: Socrates’ moral principle in the Crito is that

options.text: one may return injustice for injustice if the city erred
one must not do injustice, even in return
friends’ opinions outweigh the expert on justice
exile is always worse than death

questions.explanation: The dialogue pairs with Apology: defiance of a verdict is not a license to harm the legal order as such.

questions.prompt: A serious objection the sitting asked you to consider is that

options.text: the Laws assume a consent Socrates never actually signed
Crito is not a real person

questions.explanation: Tacit consent by remaining is the controversial lemma. Naming it is part of reading, not a refusal to read.

recapQuiz.title: Socrates: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Three sittings, one practice: definition, public examination, and the city’s claim on a life.

questions.prompt: Across Euthyphro, Apology, and Crito, a Socratic question is typically a demand for

options.text: a list of examples or a quotation from a poet as sufficient
an account that can survive ‘why?’ — what piety, wisdom, or justice is

questions.explanation: Euthyphro makes the demand explicit; Apology and Crito spend that demand in a life.

questions.prompt: The examined life in the Apology is

options.text: a private hobby Socrates would drop to live
a duty he will not trade for acquittal
identical with Crito’s plan to escape
a proof that he knows piety’s form

questions.explanation: Crito then shows that the same man will not injure the laws to save that life.

questions.prompt: The Laws’ speech in Crito is in tension with the Apology because

options.text: both texts deny that Athens has laws
he defies a jury’s verdict in one and refuses to destroy the legal order in the other
the oracle is repeated as a proof of piety

questions.explanation: That tension is the unit’s point, not a continuity error.

questions.prompt: By the end of this unit Socrates has stated the form of piety successfully.
questions.explanation: Euthyphro ends in aporia. The unit teaches the method, not a completed definition.

questions.prompt: A mistake this unit is designed to kill is that Socratic ignorance is

options.text: a method and a moral stance
a claim that nothing — including duty — can be known or cared about
distinct from the old comic slander

questions.explanation: He still claims things about death and justice. Ignorance is not nihilism.

units.title: Can virtue be taught?
units.professorNote: Meno is two sittings because the slave-boy demonstration and the distinction between knowledge and true belief are easy to rush. Do not rush them.

assignments.title: Meno: the paradox of inquiry and the slave
assignments.author: Plato (Socrates as speaker)
assignments.selection: From the opening through the geometry lesson and the theory of recollection
assignments.why: Meno wants a straight answer: can virtue be taught? Socrates wants a definition of virtue. Then the famous paradox: you cannot search for what you do not know, because you would not recognize it. The slave-boy scene is not a math class. It is Plato’s first serious bid to explain how learning is possible — recollection, the soul’s prior acquaintance with truth. You may reject recollection. You may not skip the problem it is trying to solve.
lookFor: Meno’s first definitions and why they fail (lists, parts, not the whole)
The paradox of inquiry, stated carefully
What the slave is supposed to have shown: that he ‘recollected,’ not that he was taught in the ordinary sense
questions: Does the geometry lesson actually support recollection, or only that leading questions can elicit a proof?
Restate the paradox so that it is not a cheap trick.
assignments.nextHint: The second sitting: knowledge versus true opinion, and the political sting in the tail.

quiz.title: After Meno’s paradox and the slave
quiz.intro: Learning as recollection — or at least the problem it tries to solve.

questions.prompt: Meno’s paradox of inquiry says, roughly, that

options.text: virtue is always taught in Sparta
you cannot search for what you do not know, because you would not recognize it if you found it
Socrates is too old to learn

questions.explanation: That is the paradox. Recollection is Plato’s bid to explain how learning is possible anyway.

questions.prompt: The slave-boy demonstration is offered as evidence that

options.text: anyone can be taught horsemanship in an afternoon
the boy recollects a geometrical truth rather than being merely stuffed with Socrates’ doctrine in the ordinary way

questions.explanation: You may reject recollection. You may not skip the problem. Leading questions vs recollection is the sitting’s own question.

questions.prompt: Meno’s first attempts at defining virtue fail because they

options.text: give lists or parts (virtue of a man, a woman) rather than the one form of virtue

questions.explanation: Same Socratic demand as Euthyphro: not a catalogue.

assignments.title: Meno: knowledge, true belief, and virtue
assignments.author: Plato (Socrates as speaker)
assignments.selection: From after the recollection episode to the end
assignments.why: If virtue is knowledge, it should be teachable — but Athens has no teachers of virtue in the way it has teachers of horsemanship. The distinction between knowledge and true opinion (the statues of Daedalus that run away unless tethered) is one of the most useful tools in the whole course. Right opinion can guide action; it is not yet understanding. Watch how the dialogue’s political irony undercuts a simple ‘virtue is knowledge’ slogan.
lookFor: Knowledge vs true opinion: the tethering image
Why the great Athenians could not teach their sons virtue
Whether the dialogue ends in a theory or in a deliberately unstable result
questions: If true opinion is as useful as knowledge for action, why prefer knowledge?
What would a teacher of virtue have to possess that a successful politician might lack?
assignments.nextHint: The Republic will ask what justice is in a soul and a city — and will give you the Cave.

quiz.title: After knowledge and true opinion
quiz.intro: Why tether the statues.

questions.prompt: True opinion differs from knowledge, in the Meno’s image, because

options.text: true opinion can guide action but runs away unless tethered by an account — like Daedalus’s statues
Athenians have knowledge and no opinions

questions.explanation: The tethering image is the tool the sitting named. Right opinion is not yet understanding.

questions.prompt: The political sting at the end is that

options.text: if virtue were knowledge, there should be teachers — but the great Athenians could not teach their sons
Meno becomes a sophist for pay

questions.explanation: The irony undercuts a simple ‘virtue is knowledge’ slogan even as the distinction knowledge/opinion is introduced.

questions.prompt: If true opinion is as useful as knowledge for a given action, the Meno sees no remaining reason to prefer knowledge.
questions.explanation: Usefulness in a single action is not stability or understanding. That is why the statues need tethering.

units.title: Justice, the soul, and the Cave
units.professorNote: Do not read the whole Republic. Read the argument about justice, then the metaphysics of education (sun, line, cave). That is the stretch that teaches the Platonic move.

assignments.title: Republic I: three failed accounts of justice
assignments.author: Plato
assignments.why: Book I is a Socratic demolition: Cephalus (paying debts, telling truth), Polemarchus (helping friends, harming enemies), Thrasymachus (the advantage of the stronger). You need Thrasymachus in your bones before you meet Hobbes or Nietzsche. Socrates’ replies here are not yet the full theory of justice; they are the clearing of the site. Notice that the book ends without a definition — on purpose.
lookFor: Why ‘giving back what is owed’ fails (the madman’s weapon)
Thrasymachus: justice as another’s good; the tyrant as happy
Socrates’ arguments that the unjust life is not the stronger life — and where they feel thin
questions: State Thrasymachus’s position so that it is as strong as you can make it.
Has Socrates refuted ‘might makes right,’ or only a sloppy version of it?
assignments.nextHint: Books II–IV will rebuild justice as a structure in city and soul.

quiz.title: After Republic I
quiz.intro: Thrasymachus in your bones.

questions.prompt: Thrasymachus’s challenge, at full strength, is that justice is

options.text: paying debts and telling the truth, always
the advantage of the stronger — and the unjust life can be the happier, more successful one
a Form in a separate heaven

questions.explanation: Helping friends/harming enemies is Polemarchus. Cephalus is debts and truth. Thrasymachus is the adult challenge Book I exists to put on the table.

questions.prompt: Cephalus’s account fails because

options.text: returning what is owed (the madman’s weapon) is not always just
Socrates forbids old men to speak

questions.explanation: A counterexample wrecks a definition by cases. Same move as Euthyphro.

questions.prompt: Book I ends without a definition of justice because

options.text: the demolitions are the clearing of the site; the constructive theory waits
justice is indefinable in principle, as Moore will later say of good

questions.explanation: Aporia here is architectural. Do not treat Book I as the whole Republic.

questions.prompt: Socrates’ replies in Book I already give the full theory of justice in the soul.
questions.explanation: They are not yet Books IV and VII. The sitting said so.

assignments.title: Republic II and IV: city, soul, the virtues
assignments.author: Plato
assignments.selection: Glaucon’s challenge; the origin of the city; the four virtues in the city; justice in the soul (Book IV)
assignments.pages: Stephanus 357a–367e (Glaucon/Adeimantus); then 427d–445e (virtues in city and soul). You may skim the long city-founding middle of II–III.
assignments.why: Glaucon’s Gyges ring is the adult version of Thrasymachus: why be just if you can be unjust without cost? Plato’s strategy is analogical — justice writ large in a city, then in a soul with three parts. The payoff in Book IV: justice as each part doing its work, in city and in soul. You do not need the censorship arguments of Book III for this course; you need the structure.
lookFor: Glaucon’s threefold classification of goods and where he places justice
The three parts of the soul and their civic counterparts
Justice as a structural relation, not a list of actions
questions: Does the city-soul analogy prove anything, or only illustrate a hypothesis?
If justice is psychic order, what happens to justice as a relation to other people?
assignments.nextHint: Now the Cave: what education is, if the soul has parts and the world has levels.

quiz.title: After city and soul
quiz.intro: Justice as a structure, not a list of actions.

questions.prompt: Glaucon’s Gyges story is meant to force the question

options.text: why be just if you can be unjust without cost or detection

questions.explanation: It is the adult Thrasymachus: justice as a good we want only for its consequences, unless Socrates can show otherwise.

questions.prompt: In Book IV, justice in the city is

options.text: each class doing its own work — a structural relation among parts
a complete list of legal statutes
whatever the strongest orator says that day

questions.explanation: And analogically in the soul: reason, spirit, appetite each at their work. That is the constructive definition.

questions.prompt: A worry the sitting asked you to keep is that the city–soul analogy

options.text: has no three parts in the city
may illustrate a hypothesis rather than prove that justice in a person is that structure

questions.explanation: Analogies can smuggle. Naming that is reading Plato well.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are among the four civic virtues Plato locates in the city in this stretch?

options.text: moderation as agreement about who should rule

questions.explanation: Wisdom, courage, moderation, justice — not modern economic metrics. Justice is the remaining structural virtue of each doing its work.

assignments.title: Sun, line, and Cave
assignments.author: Plato
assignments.selection: The Good as sun; the divided line; the Cave and the return
assignments.pages: Stephanus 506b–521b (end of VI through the Cave and the philosopher’s return)
assignments.why: This is the image everyone knows and almost no one reads slowly. The sun is not a pretty metaphor for ‘enlightenment.’ It is a claim about what makes knowable things knowable — the Good. The line ranks images, sensibles, mathematical thought, and dialectic. The Cave is a story about education as turning, and about the political cost of returning to the prisoners. You now have Plato’s epistemology and his politics in one stretch. That is enough Republic.
lookFor: What the sun is supposed to do for sight and generation — analogically, what the Good does for knowledge and being
The four segments of the line, with an example in each
Why the released prisoner is compelled to go back down
questions: Is the Cave a theory of knowledge, a theory of politics, or a theory of conversion — and can it be all three without confusion?
What would it mean to ‘look at the sun’ without Plato’s Forms?
assignments.nextHint: Aristotle will try to explain being and change without a separate realm of Forms.

quiz.title: After sun, line, and Cave
quiz.intro: Education as turning, and the cost of return.

questions.prompt: The sun analogy claims that the Good is to the intelligible realm as the sun is to the visible: it

options.text: is a large fire in the sky only
makes knowable things knowable (and, analogically, being ‘be’) rather than being one more object among objects

questions.explanation: The sitting: not a pretty word for ‘enlightenment.’ The Good is a source, not a thing on the wall.

questions.prompt: The divided line ranks

options.text: images, sensibles, mathematical thought, and dialectic / intellection of Forms

questions.explanation: You were asked for four segments with an example in each. That is the epistemology.

questions.prompt: The released prisoner is compelled to go back down because

options.text: education and rule, on this picture, include a political cost: returning to those still chained

questions.explanation: The Cave is politics as well as knowledge. The philosopher-king is not a careerist’s prize.

questions.prompt: The Cave is only an epistemology and has no political meaning.
questions.explanation: The sitting asked whether it can be knowledge, politics, and conversion at once.

recapQuiz.title: Republic: recap
recapQuiz.intro: From Thrasymachus’s challenge to a structure of soul and city, then to the Cave.

questions.prompt: The constructive definition of justice in the city is

options.text: each part doing its own work — analogically in the soul

questions.explanation: Book I clears the site; Book IV builds. Do not stop at Thrasymachus.

questions.prompt: Glaucon’s Gyges story forces Socrates to show that justice is

options.text: only a social contract for the weak
worth choosing even if one could be unjust without cost
unnecessary if one has a ring

questions.explanation: That is why Book I’s demolitions were not yet enough.

questions.prompt: Sun, line, and Cave together claim that

options.text: the Good is a source of knowability and being, and education is a turning — with a political cost of return
justice is the advantage of the tyrant

questions.explanation: The Cave is knowledge and politics. The unit is not ‘Plato liked allegories.’

questions.prompt: The city–soul analogy is a finished proof that a person is just exactly when a city is.
questions.explanation: It may illustrate a hypothesis. The unit asked you to keep that worry.

questions.prompt: Book I’s remaining work, after the recap of the whole unit, is best described as

options.text: the full theory of the philosopher-king
putting the adult challenge (justice as another’s good, the happier unjust life) on the table

questions.explanation: Without Thrasymachus, Books IV and VII have no enemy.

units.title: Substance, nature, and causes
units.professorNote: Two sittings: how to say what a thing is (Categories), then how change is possible without Parmenides’ contradiction (Physics II).

assignments.title: Categories 1–5: substance
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.why: Before ethics, you need Aristotle’s grammar of being. Things are said in many ways, but not chaotically: there are categories. Primary substance — this horse, this human — is the subject that qualities inhere in. That is a decision against treating universals as more real than the animals in front of you. If you later hear ‘substance’ in Descartes or Locke, this is the ancestor they are rewriting.
lookFor: Homonyms, synonyms, paronyms — why the opening is not pedantry
Primary vs secondary substance
Why substance is ‘neither said of a subject nor in a subject’
questions: What is lost if we treat ‘human’ as more real than Socrates?
How is this already a reply to a certain reading of Plato’s Forms?
assignments.nextHint: Physics II will add nature, matter/form, and the four causes.

quiz.title: After Categories 1–5
quiz.intro: This horse, not Horse-itself, as primary.

questions.prompt: Primary substance, in the Categories, is

options.text: this particular: this horse, this human — the subject qualities inhere in
whatever we can define in mathematics

questions.explanation: Neither said of a subject nor in a subject. Universals are secondary. That is the anti-separate-Forms decision.

questions.prompt: The opening on homonyms and synonyms is there because

options.text: Aristotle loves grammar for its own sake only
‘being’ and our predicates are said in many ways, and the distinctions prevent equivocation

questions.explanation: It is the grammar of being, not pedantry.

questions.prompt: On this account, the species ‘human’ is more a substance than Socrates is.
questions.explanation: Socrates is primary substance. ‘Human’ is said of him. That is the reply to a certain Platonism.

assignments.title: Physics II: nature and the four causes
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.translator: R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye
assignments.why: Nature is an inner principle of motion and rest — not a nickname for ‘everything.’ The four causes (material, formal, efficient, final) are not a dusty list; they are four answers to ‘why?’ that Parmenides and the atomists each tried to collapse. Final cause will offend you if you think modern physics. Read it as a claim about living things and artifacts first. You need this for Aquinas later, and for every later fight about teleology.
lookFor: Nature vs art: the difference between growing and being built
The four ‘becauses,’ with one example that uses all four
Why chance is not a fifth kind of cause on a par with these
questions: Can you explain a tree without a ‘that for the sake of which’?
How does form-in-matter let Aristotle keep change without Parmenides’ contradiction?
assignments.nextHint: Ethics: what the human ergon is, and what a virtue is.

quiz.title: After Physics II.1–3
quiz.intro: Four answers to ‘why?’

questions.prompt: Nature, for Aristotle here, is

options.text: an inner principle of motion and rest in the thing itself — unlike an artifact, whose principle is in the artisan

questions.explanation: Growing vs being built. That distinction carries the four causes.

questions.prompt: The four causes are best thought of as

options.text: four kinds of event in a lab
four answers to ‘why?’ (material, formal, efficient, final)

questions.explanation: A house: bricks, the plan, the builder, shelter. One example using all four was the assignment.

questions.prompt: Final cause will offend a certain modern ear because

options.text: it says some explanations cite that-for-the-sake-of-which, not only pushes from behind

questions.explanation: You were told to hear it first in living things and artifacts, not to shout ‘physics refuted this’ before understanding the claim.

units.title: Happiness, virtue, wisdom
units.professorNote: Three sittings, not a survey of the corpus. Happiness and virtue first; then a sliver of Metaphysics so ‘first philosophy’ is not a rumor; then demonstration so you see what Aristotle thinks knowledge is.

assignments.title: Nicomachean Ethics I: happiness
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.selection: Book I, especially I.1–7 (the good, eudaimonia, the function argument)
assignments.pages: NE I.1–I.7 (Bekker 1094a–1098b); skim I.8–13 if you have time
assignments.why: Every craft aims at some good; the highest good for a human life is eudaimonia — not a mood, but a complete activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. The function argument is the hinge: if a human has an ergon, it has to do with reason. You may reject the idea that humans have a function. You must first hear it as Aristotle states it, not as a later sermon about ‘purpose.’
lookFor: The difference between eudaimonia and pleasure, honor, or money
The function (ergon) argument, premise by premise
Why a complete life is required — why one swallow does not make a spring
questions: What is eudaimonia, on this account, in words you would use of a living person?
Why does Aristotle think a human has a function at all?
assignments.nextHint: Book II: virtue as a mean in the soul’s habits.

quiz.title: After Nicomachean Ethics I
quiz.intro: Eudaimonia is not a mood.

questions.prompt: Eudaimonia in NE I is

options.text: a pleasant feeling that comes and goes
a complete activity of the soul in accordance with virtue (over a complete life)
honor from the city, full stop

questions.explanation: Not pleasure, honor, or wealth as the highest good. Activity, virtue, completeness of life.

questions.prompt: The function (ergon) argument claims that

options.text: if a human has a function, it concerns reason, and the good life is performing that function well

questions.explanation: You may reject ‘function.’ You must first hear it as stated — the sitting’s rule.

questions.prompt: One swallow makes a spring: a single happy day makes a eudaimōn life.
questions.explanation: Aristotle’s own proverb in this book: a complete life is required.

questions.prompt: The highest good is sought as

options.text: that for the sake of which other things are chosen — complete and self-sufficient in the relevant sense

questions.explanation: The architectonic opening: crafts nest; the highest end does not nest inside another.

assignments.title: Nicomachean Ethics II: moral virtue
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.selection: Book II entire (virtue as habit; the mean)
assignments.why: Virtue is not a feeling and not a mere capacity. It is a hexis — a stable disposition — formed by action, aiming at a mean relative to us, defined by reason as the prudent person would define it. The mean is not mediocrity; it is hitting the mark in fear, anger, giving, truth-telling. This is the ethics the Stoics will radicalize and Kant will refuse to found on habit.
lookFor: Why virtues of character are acquired by habituation
The mean ‘relative to us’ — not a geometric midpoint
The list of virtues as a map of situations, not a personality test
questions: Can a person know the mean and still not be virtuous? What is missing?
Pick one virtue and say what the two vices are — and why the mean is not ‘being moderate about everything.’
assignments.nextHint: A short look at first philosophy, then demonstration — so ethics is not floating free of Aristotle’s idea of knowledge.

quiz.title: After Nicomachean Ethics II
quiz.intro: The mean is not mediocrity.

questions.prompt: A moral virtue, here, is

options.text: a stable disposition (hexis) formed by habituation, aiming at a mean relative to us, as the prudent person would define it

questions.explanation: Not a feeling, not a mere capacity. Habit, mean, reason — the three notes of the sitting.

questions.prompt: The mean is ‘relative to us’ because

options.text: there is no truth in ethics
hitting the mark in fear or anger is not a geometric midpoint the same for every body and situation

questions.explanation: Mediocrity is the cartoon. Courage is not half-cowardice.

questions.prompt: Knowing what the mean is already makes a person virtuous.
questions.explanation: The sitting asked what is missing: habituation, the hexis. Knowledge without character is not yet virtue of character.

assignments.title: Metaphysics: wonder, wisdom, being qua being
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.selection: I.1–2 (wisdom, experience, wonder) and IV.1–2 (being qua being; focal meaning)
assignments.why: All humans by nature desire to know. Wisdom is knowledge of first causes and principles. Book IV then names the science that studies being insofar as it is being — not numbers, not nature in motion, but what it is to be. ‘Being is said in many ways’ but not as a heap of homonyms: there is a focal meaning around substance. This sliver is enough to make later ontology recognizable.
lookFor: The ladder: sensation, memory, experience, art, wisdom
Why first philosophy is not physics
Focal meaning: how ‘healthy’ helps explain how ‘being’ is said in many ways
questions: What would it mean to study being without studying some particular kind of being?
How does this continue, and refuse, the Cave’s ranking of knowledge?
assignments.nextHint: Posterior Analytics: what a demonstration is, and why not everything can be demonstrated.

quiz.title: After Metaphysics I and IV (openings)
quiz.intro: Being is said in many ways — with a focus.

questions.prompt: Wisdom, in Metaphysics I.1–2, is

options.text: knowledge of first causes and principles, beginning in wonder

questions.explanation: The ladder sensation–memory–experience–art–wisdom, and the claim that we desire to know by nature.

questions.prompt: ‘Being qua being’ means, most nearly,

options.text: the study of what it is to be, not of some particular moving kind as physics studies it
theology in Anselm’s later sense only

questions.explanation: First philosophy is not physics. That is the sliver you were assigned.

questions.prompt: Focal meaning (as with ‘healthy’) is used to say that

options.text: all uses of ‘being’ are unrelated puns
‘being’ is said in many ways but around a focus — substance

questions.explanation: Not a heap of homonyms. The Categories’ primary substance is still in the room.

assignments.title: Posterior Analytics I.1–3: demonstration and first principles
assignments.author: Aristotle
assignments.why: You cannot demonstrate everything: some things are first. Knowledge of a conclusion is through demonstration; the principles are known another way (nous, induction). This is the ancestor of every later fight about foundations — Descartes’ clear and distinct ideas, Hume’s missing impression, Moore’s intuitions. Read it as a constraint: a science has a shape, and infinite regress is not a shape.
lookFor: What a demonstration is (syllogism from true, primary, immediate premises)
The regress problem if every premise must itself be demonstrated
The difference between knowing that and knowing why
questions: If first principles are not demonstrated, how are they more than prejudices?
What would Hume say is missing from this picture of knowledge?
assignments.nextHint: The schools after Aristotle will treat philosophy as a way of life under empire — starting with Epicurus.

quiz.title: After demonstration and first principles
quiz.intro: You cannot demonstrate everything.

questions.prompt: A demonstration, here, is

options.text: a syllogism from true, primary, immediate premises that give the why

questions.explanation: Knowledge of a conclusion through demonstration has a shape. Infinite regress is not a shape.

questions.prompt: First principles are known

options.text: another way — not by demonstrating them from still prior demonstrations (nous / induction in Aristotle’s sense)
only by divine revelation in this treatise

questions.explanation: If every premise needed demonstration, nothing would be known as science. That is the regress the sitting named.

questions.prompt: Aristotle thinks a science can be a chain of demonstrations with no undemonstrated starting points.
questions.explanation: That is exactly what I.1–3 refuse.

recapQuiz.title: Aristotle: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Happiness, virtue, wisdom, and what a science needs in order to start.

questions.prompt: Eudaimonia in NE I is

options.text: activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life
the Form of the Good as Plato locates it

questions.explanation: NE II then says what a virtue of character is. Keep the pair.

questions.prompt: The mean is not mediocrity because

options.text: it is a geometric midpoint the same for every body
it is hitting the mark relative to us, as the phronimos would judge — courage is not half-cowardice
knowledge without habituation is already virtue

questions.explanation: Hexis plus reason. That was NE II’s lookFor.

questions.prompt: First philosophy studies

options.text: being qua being — with ‘being’ said in many ways around a focus (substance)

questions.explanation: Metaphysics I and IV openings, after the Categories’ primary substance.

questions.prompt: Demonstration cannot go back forever because

options.text: some principles must be known another way (nous / induction), or nothing is scientifically known

questions.explanation: Posterior Analytics I.1–3. The unit’s last sitting.

questions.prompt: On the Categories, the species ‘human’ is more substance than Socrates.
questions.explanation: Primary substance is the particular. That decision still governs the metaphysics sitting.

eras.title: Hellenistic schools
eras.intro: After Aristotle, philosophy becomes a way of life under uncertainty and empire. Epicureans reduce fear by a physics of atoms and a careful hedonism. Stoics relocate freedom inside what is up to us. Skeptics suspend judgment to find quiet. You are learning three answers to the same question: how to live when the cosmos will not arrange itself around your wishes.

units.title: The Garden: pleasure without frenzy
units.professorNote: Epicurus is short and lucent; Lucretius is the physics and the therapy of death. Read them as one argument in two voices.

assignments.title: Letter to Menoeceus
assignments.author: Epicurus
assignments.why: This is the cleanest statement of Epicurean ethics you will get. Pleasure is the end, but not the banquet: natural and necessary desires, the limit of pain, the claim that death is nothing to us because when we are, death is not. Prudence is called more precious than philosophy itself. Read it against Aristotle’s eudaimonia: a rival account of a complete life, stripped of civic grandeur.
lookFor: The classification of desires (natural/necessary vs empty)
Why death is ‘nothing to us’ — the symmetry of not-yet and no-longer
How prudence, not luxury, produces ataraxia
questions: Is this hedonism, or a discipline against hedonism as the many practice it?
What must be true of the soul for death to be nothing to us?
assignments.nextHint: Lucretius will give the atomic physics that is supposed to make this courage possible.

quiz.title: After the Letter to Menoeceus
quiz.intro: Pleasure as a disciplined end, not a banquet.

questions.prompt: Epicurus classifies desires so that ataraxia is possible. Empty desires are those that

options.text: are natural and necessary, like hunger
have no natural limit and are produced by false beliefs about what we need

questions.explanation: Natural/necessary vs empty is the letter’s practical physics of the soul. Unlimited wants cannot be satisfied, so they cannot be the end.

questions.prompt: ‘Death is nothing to us’ depends on the claim that

options.text: the soul survives and is rewarded
when we exist, death is not present, and when death is present, we do not
the unborn suffer the way the dead do

questions.explanation: No subject remains to be harmed. That is why the letter can treat death-fear as a confusion, not a fate.

questions.prompt: Prudence is called more precious than philosophy because

options.text: it is the practical wisdom that chooses among pleasures and produces a stable life

questions.explanation: The letter’s hedonism is a discipline: the many’s frenzy is exactly what prudence refuses.

questions.prompt: On this letter, every pleasure is to be pursued as it arises.
questions.explanation: Some pleasures bring greater pains. The classification of desires is the filter.

assignments.title: Lucretius I: nothing comes from nothing
assignments.author: Lucretius
assignments.selection: Book I: atoms, void, the ban on generation from nothing
assignments.pages: De rerum natura Book I (opening through atoms and void; Leonard)
assignments.why: Lucretius turns Epicurus into Latin verse so that fear of the gods and of death can be treated as errors in physics. Nothing comes from nothing; nothing passes into nothing; there is void as well as body. You have heard this strategy since the atomists. Now it is in the service of a life: if the world is atoms, the thunderbolt is not a judgment.
lookFor: The argument that something cannot arise from nothing
Why void is required for motion
How physics is already ethics here — a therapy of fear
questions: What religious fear is supposed to dissolve if Book I is true?
Is ‘nothing from nothing’ a physical claim, a logical claim, or both?
assignments.nextHint: Book III: why death cannot harm the one who dies.

quiz.title: After Lucretius I
quiz.intro: Physics as a therapy of fear.

questions.prompt: Lucretius argues that something cannot arise from nothing because otherwise

options.text: anything could come from anything, and there would be no need of seed or season
Aristotle’s four causes would be confirmed

questions.explanation: The ‘nothing from nothing’ rule is a constraint on explanation: generation needs a determinate source.

questions.prompt: Void is required, as in the older atomists, because

options.text: body cannot move or yield if there is no empty interval
void is the same as the soul

questions.explanation: Motion needs somewhere to go. Book I puts Eleatic pressure to work for Epicurean physics.

questions.prompt: In this book, the physics is already ethics because

options.text: if thunder and plague are atomic, they need not be read as divine punishment

questions.explanation: The sitting: a therapy of fear. Superstition is a mistaken physics.

assignments.title: Lucretius III: death is nothing to us
assignments.author: Lucretius
assignments.selection: Book III: the mortal soul; the argument that death is not an evil
assignments.pages: De rerum natura Book III (the soul’s mortality and the consolation)
assignments.why: If the soul is a fine atomic structure that dissolves, there is no surviving subject to suffer after death. The ‘now we are, death is not’ argument returns with images: the unborn, the broken vessel. You may reject materialism and still need to say why this consolation fails. That is the sitting.
lookFor: Why the soul must be bodily if it is to move a body
The no-surviving-subject argument
The appeal to the time before birth as analogue of the time after death
questions: Does the argument show that death is not bad, or only that post-mortem experience is impossible?
What would a Platonic dualist have to deny in Book III’s opening moves?
assignments.nextHint: The Stoics will relocate the good inside assent, not in the dissolution of fear by physics.

quiz.title: After Lucretius III
quiz.intro: No surviving subject, no posthumous harm.

questions.prompt: The soul must be bodily, on Lucretius’s opening moves, because

options.text: it affects and is affected with the body — it moves a body and suffers with it

questions.explanation: An incorporeal soul could not shove atoms. Mortality of mind follows from its atomic structure.

questions.prompt: Death cannot harm the one who dies, in the central argument, because

options.text: the compound dissolves, so there is no remaining subject of experience
the unborn are happier than we are

questions.explanation: The assignment distinguished this from a proof that death is not bad in every sense — it shows the impossibility of post-mortem experience.

questions.prompt: The time before birth is invoked as

options.text: an analogue: we do not lament the ages before we existed, so why lament the ages after?
a proof that the soul is immortal

questions.explanation: Symmetry with the unborn is the consolation-image. A dualist must deny the soul’s dissolution.

questions.prompt: Book III claims that death is bad because it deprives us of future pleasures we would have enjoyed.
questions.explanation: That deprivation view is exactly what the no-subject argument is meant to undercut — or at least to recast.

recapQuiz.title: Garden: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Pleasure disciplined, and a physics that is already a therapy.

questions.prompt: Epicurus’s letter and Lucretius I–III together claim that

options.text: fear of gods and of death rests on a false physics, and empty desires cannot be satisfied
the city is the highest good as in Aristotle’s Politics

questions.explanation: Ethics first (Menoeceus), then the atomic reasons (Lucretius).

questions.prompt: Death is nothing to us, in this school, because

options.text: no subject remains to suffer — Book III’s dissolution of the soul-compound

questions.explanation: The letter’s slogan gets Lucretius’s argument.

questions.prompt: Void in Lucretius I is required for
questions.explanation: Same Eleatic pressure as the earlier atomists, now in the service of a life.

questions.prompt: This unit’s hedonism is identical with pursuing every pleasure as it arises.
questions.explanation: Natural vs empty desires, and pleasures that cost greater pains, are the filter.

questions.prompt: A remaining objection the sittings asked you to keep is that

options.text: showing there is no post-mortem experience may not yet show that death cannot be bad as deprivation

questions.explanation: Book III’s seminar question. Recap it, don’t erase it.

units.title: Stoic discipline
units.professorNote: Epictetus first (the handbook), then Marcus (the notebook). The theory is simple; the difficulty is the use. Do not romanticize either man.

assignments.title: Enchiridion 1–29: what is up to us
assignments.author: Epictetus
assignments.selection: Opening half of the Manual, especially §§1–11, 15–21
assignments.pages: Enchiridion §§1–29 (stop before the later social maxims if pressed for time)
assignments.why: The first sentence is the whole school: some things are up to us, some are not. Assent, impulse, desire — these can be trained. Body, property, reputation are not. Happiness is not getting the world to obey; it is not demanding that it obey. Read this as a theory of freedom after Aristotle’s civic virtue: the slave Epictetus is claiming a freedom a consul might lack.
lookFor: The dichotomy of control, stated without slogan
How desire and aversion are to be relocated
What ‘follow nature’ means when nature includes other people’s injustice
questions: Is this wisdom, or a way of calling losses unimportant so they hurt less?
Can a Stoic still have duties to others if their welfare is ‘not up to us’?
assignments.nextHint: Finish the Manual, then watch an emperor try to live it.

quiz.title: After Enchiridion (opening)
quiz.intro: What is up to us.

questions.prompt: The handbook’s first cut is between

options.text: what is up to us (judgment, impulse, desire) and what is not (body, property, reputation, office)
pleasure and pain as Epicurus ranked them

questions.explanation: Freedom is relocated inside assent. Confusing the two classes is the source of disturbance.

questions.prompt: If something is not up to you, the disciplined response is

options.text: to pretend it is, so you stay ambitious
not to treat it as good or evil in the strict sense — not to stake your eudaimonia on it

questions.explanation: The sitting is not quietism as a mood. It is a classification of value.

questions.prompt: Epictetus teaches that you can, with enough effort, make other people’s opinions up to you.
questions.explanation: Reputation is listed among things not up to us. The work is on the use of impressions.

assignments.title: Enchiridion 30–53: roles, shame, and the philosopher
assignments.author: Epictetus
assignments.why: The second half applies the dichotomy to roles (father, citizen), to insult, to divination, to the wish to be a philosopher in appearance. Notice how social life is not abandoned: you play the role well, without needing the world’s applause. This is the ancestor of later ‘interior’ freedom — and of every cheap self-help version. Keep the cheap version out.
lookFor: How roles (son, citizen) can bind without making outcomes ‘up to us’
The treatment of insult and reputation
What a philosopher looks like when not performing philosophy
questions: Does ‘play your role’ collapse into conventional obedience?
Where would Epictetus tell you to resist a law, if ever?
assignments.nextHint: Marcus writes the same discipline from the other end of the social scale.

quiz.title: After Enchiridion (use)
quiz.intro: Impressions, roles, and the inner citadel in practice.

questions.prompt: When a troubling impression appears, the handbook’s move is to

options.text: immediately assent that the world is bad
pause and test: is this something up to me, and what has been added by my judgment?

questions.explanation: Assent is the free act. The world does not have to change for the passion to lose its necessity.

questions.prompt: Playing a role (child, citizen, guest) in these later chapters means

options.text: performing the duties of the part assigned, without demanding that the script be rewritten

questions.explanation: The sitting asked you not to romanticize: duty in a role is not a feeling of serenity.

questions.prompt: A plausible misreading to refuse is that Stoicism here is

options.text: a promise that nothing painful will happen to the body
an account of what is up to us
a handbook for use, not a metaphysics textbook

questions.explanation: Body and death remain not up to you. The good is not the body’s immunity.

assignments.title: Marcus Aurelius, Books II–IV
assignments.author: Marcus Aurelius
assignments.why: These are notes to himself, not a treatise. That is the point: you see the Stoic machinery under fatigue — death, the court, the body’s complaint. Look for the view from above, the reminder that you are a part of the whole, and the refusal to be stained by another’s judgment. Compare the tone with Epictetus: same doctrine, different temperature.
lookFor: The ‘view from above’ and what it is for
How he talks himself out of anger without denying that people act badly
Death as a natural process, not a catastrophe
questions: Is this piety toward the cosmos, or a technique for an overworked administrator?
What would Epicurus dispute in Marcus’s picture of the whole?
assignments.nextHint: Skepticism will ask whether you should assent to any of these pictures of nature.

quiz.title: After Marcus (selected books)
quiz.intro: A notebook, not a system — but the same cut.

questions.prompt: Marcus repeatedly returns to the thought that

options.text: he can control the empire’s outcomes
other people’s wrongdoing and cosmic events lie outside his ruling faculty, which he can keep just

questions.explanation: The Meditations apply Epictetus’s cut in an emperor’s isolation. Do not turn them into a brand.

questions.prompt: When Marcus writes of nature or the Whole, he is typically

options.text: locating himself as a part among parts — so that anger at the universe is a confusion of scale
quoting Lucretius with approval of atoms only

questions.explanation: Cosmopolitan belonging is the metaphysical background of the notebook’s ethics.

questions.prompt: The Meditations are best read as proofs intended to convince a hostile jury.
questions.explanation: They are spiritual exercises. The quiz checks whether you found the repeated moves, not a treatise’s lemmas.

recapQuiz.title: Stoics: recap
recapQuiz.intro: What is up to us, from handbook to notebook.

questions.prompt: The shared Stoic cut in this unit is between

options.text: what is up to us (judgment, assent) and what is not (body, office, others’ acts)
pleasure and ataraxia as Epicurus ranks them

questions.explanation: Epictetus states it; Marcus applies it under an empire.

questions.prompt: Testing impressions matters because

options.text: passion follows a judgment that something not up to you is good or evil
the handbook is only for slaves in a legal sense

questions.explanation: Assent is the free act. Roles are duties, not a feeling of calm.

questions.prompt: A misreading this unit refuses is that Stoicism

options.text: promises that the body will not be harmed if you are wise

questions.explanation: Marcus still dies; Epictetus still has a body. The good is not immunity.

questions.prompt: The Meditations are best used as a system of lemmas like Spinoza’s Ethics.
questions.explanation: They are a notebook of repeated moves. The unit taught you to find the moves.

questions.prompt: Compared with the Garden, the Stoic good is

options.text: also a classification of desires for food
located in the quality of the ruling faculty’s use, not in the atomic dissolution of fear alone
a proof that physics is unnecessary

questions.explanation: That is why the era ordered Garden then Porch.

units.title: Skepticism as a way
units.professorNote: Sextus is not Hume. Pyrrhonism aims at quiet by withholding assent, not at a theory that nothing can be known. Catch that difference.

assignments.title: Sextus: what skepticism is
assignments.author: Sextus Empiricus
assignments.work: Pyrrhonic Sketches (Outlines of Pyrrhonism), Book I
assignments.selection: Book I of the Pyrrhonic Sketches as Patrick translates it
assignments.pages: Outlines Book I (definition of skepticism, the modes, ataraxia as the aim)
assignments.why: Skepticism is an ability to set appearances against appearances so that one suspends judgment and a quiet follows. It is not the dogma ‘nothing can be known’ — that would be another position. The tropes (modes) are tools, not a metaphysics. You will need this when Descartes tries to outflank the skeptic, and when Hume claims a mitigated version.
lookFor: Skepticism as an ability (dunamis), not a thesis
Why ‘nothing is known’ would be dogmatic
Ataraxia as the point of epoche, not a side effect the skeptic forgot to want
questions: Can a skeptic live, if action seems to require belief?
How does this differ from the Academic skepticism Hume later names?
assignments.nextHint: Plotinus will climb the other way: not suspension, but ascent to the One.

quiz.title: After Outlines of Pyrrhonism I
quiz.intro: Suspension, not a secret dogma.

questions.prompt: The Pyrrhonist’s advertised goal in Book I is

options.text: ataraxia following epochē — suspension of judgment on non-evident matters
to found a physics of atoms

questions.explanation: Quiet comes after suspension, not after a rival metaphysics. That is the school’s claim.

questions.prompt: The modes (tropes) function as

options.text: demonstrations that the skeptic has a hidden doctrine of truth
ways of opposing appearances to appearances so that assent is withheld

questions.explanation: Equipollence: equally strong on both sides. The skeptic lives by appearance without claiming a criterion of the non-evident.

questions.prompt: A serious question the sitting left you with is whether the skeptic

options.text: can live by appearances while claiming to suspend on all belief — or smuggles beliefs in

questions.explanation: The ‘apraxia’ charge is the old objection. Sextus’s answer is life by the apparent, not dogma.

questions.prompt: Sextus’s Book I is mainly a biography of Pyrrho’s travels.
questions.explanation: It is a method: tropes, criterion, and the promise of quiet.

eras.title: Late antiquity and inwardness
eras.intro: Platonism becomes a metaphysics of procession from the One; Christianity inherits that ladder and turns it inward. Augustine is the hinge: the restless heart, the divided will, and time as a distension of the soul. You are watching philosophy learn to describe a first-person interior that Plato’s Cave only sketched.

units.title: From the One to consolation
units.professorNote: Plotinus for the structure of reality; Boethius for the imprisoned intellectual who still wants Providence to make sense.

assignments.title: Plotinus: the three hypostases
assignments.author: Plotinus
assignments.selection: The stretch on the One, Intellect, and Soul in the hosted MacKenna selection
assignments.pages: Ennead V material as hosted (The Divine Mind / three hypostases)
assignments.why: Reality proceeds: the One beyond being, Intellect that thinks the Forms, Soul that looks both ways. This is Plato’s Good rewritten as a cascade. Augustine will read the Platonists and say they saw the country of truth but not the way. You only need the three levels and the idea that the lower is an image of the higher — not the whole Enneads.
lookFor: Why the One is not an intellect among others
Intellect as the realm of Forms — thinking and being together
