Soul’s double look: toward Intellect and toward the sensible
questions: Is this a religious mysticism, a metaphysics, or both without remainder?
What happens to the Cave’s prisoner if the ascent is now ontological, not only educational?
assignments.nextHint: Boethius will ask how a good providence and apparent fortune can coexist.

quiz.title: After Plotinus (selected Enneads)
quiz.intro: The One, Intellect, Soul — not a fourth god.

questions.prompt: In the Plotinian cascade, the One is

options.text: a being among beings, with parts
beyond being and intellect, the source from which Intellect and Soul proceed without emptying it

questions.explanation: The sitting: hypostases as a metaphysics of procession, not a committee of deities.

questions.prompt: Soul’s philosophical problem here is

options.text: how a unity can be the life of a many — turning toward Intellect vs dispersing into bodies

questions.explanation: Ascent is conversion of attention, continuous with Plato’s Cave but now as a cosmology.

questions.prompt: Matter, on this picture, is a positive evil substance equal to the One.
questions.explanation: Typical Plotinian line: matter as privation or last outflow, not a rival first principle. (Keep to the selected pages’ emphasis on hypostases.)

assignments.title: Boethius: Fortune and the true good
assignments.author: Boethius
assignments.selection: Book I (the complaint) and Book III (the true good)
assignments.why: A condemned man is visited by Philosophy, who diagnoses his forgetfulness of his true country. Book III argues that happiness is not Fortune’s gifts but the highest good, which is God — and that all seek it even in their errors. You are between Stoic interiority and medieval theism. Keep Lady Philosophy’s tone: not comfort as softness, but a reordering of what counts as good.
lookFor: The diagnosis: he has forgotten who he is
Fortune’s wheel versus a good that cannot be taken
How Book III identifies happiness with the highest good / God
questions: Does this console, or does it change the subject from injustice to metaphysics?
What would Lucretius say is false in the identification of the good with God?
assignments.nextHint: Augustine will make the turn inward: evil, will, time.

quiz.title: After Consolation (I and III)
quiz.intro: Fortune’s wheel, and where the good actually sits.

questions.prompt: Lady Philosophy’s opening work in Book I is to

options.text: diagnose his exile as a confusion about what is truly his, and about Fortune
prove the Forms in Aristotle’s sense

questions.explanation: The prison is the occasion; the disease is mislocated good.

questions.prompt: Book III’s argument about happiness is that

options.text: wealth, office, and fame are complete goods
partial goods (wealth, honor, power, pleasure) cannot be the true good because they fail of self-sufficiency and unity

questions.explanation: The sitting: a Platonic-Aristotelian inventory of false goods, then the turn to the highest good.

questions.prompt: A reader who stops at ‘everything happens for the best’ has

options.text: missed the work of distinguishing providence, fate, and the location of beatitude — slogans are not the consolation

questions.explanation: The assignment is the argument, not a proverb.

units.title: Augustine: evil, will, time
units.professorNote: Three sittings in the Confessions. Do not read them as autobiography only. Each book is a philosophical experiment.

assignments.title: Confessions VII: Platonists and evil
assignments.author: Augustine of Hippo
assignments.why: Augustine finds in ‘the books of the Platonists’ the Word, but not the Word made flesh. More important for philosophy: evil as privation, not a rival substance. If God is, and is good, evil cannot be a thing with being of its own. This is the metaphysical move against Manichaeism. You will hear it again whenever someone says evil is a ‘nothing’ — and you should remember how much work that claim is doing.
lookFor: What the Platonists gave him, and what they did not
Evil as privation of good, not a positive substance
The remaining problem: if evil is nothing, why does it weigh on a life?
questions: Does calling evil a privation explain cruelty, or only block a dualist cosmology?
Why is the Incarnation, on his telling, something philosophy did not deliver?
assignments.nextHint: Book VIII: the will that will not will.

quiz.title: After Confessions VII
quiz.intro: Evil as privation, not a rival substance.

questions.prompt: In Book VII, a central metaphysical claim about evil is that

options.text: evil is a positive substance equal to God
evil is a privation of good in a will or nature that remains, as being, from God
matter is created by an evil demiurge
God authors sin as a thing

questions.explanation: Manichaean dualism is the foil. If God is the source of all that is, evil cannot be a co-eternal stuff.

questions.prompt: Augustine’s intellectual conversion in this book includes

options.text: help from ‘Platonist’ books toward an incorporeal God and a non-Manichaean account of evil — still short of the will’s healing
becoming a bishop in the same chapter

questions.explanation: The sitting: metaphysics first; Book VIII is the will. Do not collapse them.

questions.prompt: Book VII already narrates the garden scene of conversion of will.
questions.explanation: That is Book VIII. VII is the intellectual problem of God and evil.

assignments.title: Confessions VIII: the divided will
assignments.author: Augustine of Hippo
assignments.why: He knows what to do and does not do it. The will is split: two wills, neither complete. This is not Aristotle’s akrasia as a lapse of reason’s rule; it is a wound in the will itself. The garden, the child’s voice, the taking up of the book — whatever you make of the conversion scene, the philosophical payload is the analysis of not being able to will wholly. Later freedom debates live here.
lookFor: The ‘two wills’ and why neither is a second substance
Habit (consuetudo) as a chain
What actually ends the deadlock in the narrative — and whether that is an argument
questions: Is a divided will still one agent, or two?
What would Epictetus say is missing from Augustine’s account of not doing what one sees?
assignments.nextHint: Book XI: what time is, if only the present is.

quiz.title: After Confessions VIII
quiz.intro: Two wills, and a will that cannot will itself whole.

questions.prompt: The ‘two wills’ analysis describes

options.text: a divided will that both wants and does not want the same conversion — not a second nature as the Manichees claimed

questions.explanation: The sitting: inner conflict without dualist metaphysics. Habit and consent are the drama.

questions.prompt: The garden scene is philosophically important because

options.text: it is only autobiography with no argument
the will’s turning is narrated as something that cannot be produced by more information alone — grace and example (the child’s song, the friends) enter the story
it repeats Book VII’s Platonism word for word

questions.explanation: You were asked to watch a will, not a theorem. Still: it is a philosophical claim about what knowledge cannot do.

questions.prompt: A plausible misreading is that Augustine simply

options.text: chooses Christianity because it is more useful for a career
distinguishes knowing the good from doing it

questions.explanation: The book is not career advice. It is the failure of a divided will to close itself.

assignments.title: Confessions XI: what is time?
assignments.author: Augustine of Hippo
assignments.why: If no one asks him, he knows; if he wishes to explain, he does not. Past and future are not; the present has no duration. Time is measured in the soul as memory, attention, expectation — a distension. This is one of the origin-points of philosophy of time. Read it as a problem forced by Genesis (‘in the beginning’) and by the phenomenology of reciting a psalm.
lookFor: Why past and future seem not to be
The threefold present: memory, attention, expectation
Time as distension of the soul (distentio animi)
questions: If time is in the soul, is there time without a created mind?
Does the psalm example measure time, or only the soul’s activity?
assignments.nextHint: Medieval philosophy will ask whether reason can prove what faith believes — starting with Anselm.

quiz.title: After Confessions XI
quiz.intro: Time as distension of the soul.

questions.prompt: Augustine’s puzzle is that

options.text: we speak of past and future, yet the past is no longer and the future is not yet — so where is time?

questions.explanation: The famous ‘if no one asks me, I know’ opening is this puzzle.

questions.prompt: His constructive suggestion is that time is

options.text: a distension of the soul: memory, attention, expectation holding past, present, and future
identical with the motion of the heavens only, with no soul
unreal in every sense, so prayer is pointless

questions.explanation: The sitting: not a physics paper. It is how a creature measures and lives time before an eternal God.

questions.prompt: On this account, God is in time the way we are, only longer.
questions.explanation: The contrast with divine eternity is the point of measuring our distension against what does not pass.

recapQuiz.title: Augustine: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Evil, will, and time — three inward problems, not one memoir.

questions.prompt: Book VII’s claim about evil is that

options.text: evil is privation of good, against Manichaean dualism
time is a container God sits in

questions.explanation: Keep VII distinct from VIII. Intellect first.

questions.prompt: Book VIII’s two wills describe

options.text: a divided will that cannot close itself by more information alone

questions.explanation: The garden is the drama of consent and habit, not a repeat of Platonist books.

questions.prompt: Book XI locates time, constructively, in

options.text: the soul’s distension: memory, attention, expectation

questions.explanation: The puzzle of past and future is the opening; distension is the proposal.

questions.prompt: These three books are interchangeable chapters on the same thesis.
questions.explanation: Evil, will, and time are three problems. Collapsing them is the usual skim.

questions.prompt: Relative to Plotinus, Augustine’s conversion story adds

options.text: a will and a time that Greek hypostases did not narrate as confession

questions.explanation: The unit sits after platonic ascent for that reason.

eras.title: Medieval reason and revelation
eras.intro: Faith seeks understanding: Anselm tries to prove God from the concept alone; Aquinas insists we start from the world. In between, Averroes and Maimonides force Latin Christendom to say how philosophy and law/scripture can share a truth. The move to learn is not ‘the Middle Ages believed in God.’ It is how argument, authority, and demonstration are supposed to fit.

units.title: Anselm’s argument and the Fool
units.professorNote: Read the Proslogion as a prayer that is also a proof. Then let Gaunilo object. Do not skip the objection.

assignments.title: Proslogion 2–4: that than which none greater
assignments.author: Anselm of Canterbury
assignments.selection: Chapters 2–4 (with the preface so you hear ‘faith seeking understanding’)
assignments.pages: Proslogium chs. 2–4 (Deane); hosted file includes Gaunilo — stop before Gaunilo for this sitting
assignments.why: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought. The Fool understands the words; what exists in the understanding and in reality is greater than what exists in the understanding alone; therefore God exists in reality. This is not a cosmological climb from motion. It is a claim about what the concept already contains. Aquinas will reject the strategy. Descartes will revive a cousin of it. Get Anselm’s actual steps, not the cartoon.
lookFor: The definition: ‘that than which nothing greater can be conceived’
The move from being in the understanding to being in reality
Why the Fool is said to understand what he denies
questions: Where, exactly, could a reasonable person refuse the step to extra-mental existence?
Is this a proof, a clarification of faith, or a spiritual exercise?
assignments.nextHint: Gaunilo will try the same form with a lost island.

text.locator: Proslogium (hosted file opens on the debate; read Anselm’s argument first)

quiz.title: After the Proslogion’s argument
quiz.intro: That than which nothing greater can be thought.

questions.prompt: Anselm’s formula for God in the argument is

options.text: the most powerful being in the universe as a fact of astronomy
that than which nothing greater can be thought
the unmoved mover as in Physics
whatever the fool says in his heart

questions.explanation: The sitting is the formula and what it is supposed to do — not a later textbook label alone.

questions.prompt: The argument’s controversial step is that

options.text: existence in reality is greater than existence in the understanding alone, so the greatest conceivable cannot be only in the understanding
the Bible already contains a proof

questions.explanation: Even if you reject the step, you must state it. ‘Faith seeking understanding’ is the frame, not a skip.

questions.prompt: Anselm presents the argument as a replacement for faith.
questions.explanation: The Proslogion is fides quaerens intellectum: understanding sought from within faith, not a cold start from nowhere.

assignments.title: Gaunilo’s lost island and Anselm’s reply
assignments.author: Gaunilo and Anselm
assignments.work: In Behalf of the Fool; Anselm’s reply
assignments.pages: Hosted sections: Gaunilo, then Anselm’s reply
assignments.why: If the form worked, a most perfect island would exist. Anselm’s reply: the form is not a recipe for any ‘greatest X’; it attaches to a being whose non-existence cannot be conceived. Whether that saves the argument is the question. You are learning how ontological arguments live or die by the uniqueness of their subject.
lookFor: The lost-island parody: what it copies and what it hopes to break
Anselm’s claim that God alone cannot be thought not to exist
Whether ‘greater’ is being used evaluatively or ontologically
questions: Does the island fail because islands are contingent, or because ‘greatest island’ is incoherent?
If you had to side with one of them after this sitting, whom, and on which lemma?
assignments.nextHint: Averroes: whether the Law commands philosophy.

quiz.title: After Gaunilo and the reply
quiz.intro: Lost islands, and whether the formula is special.

questions.prompt: Gaunilo’s ‘lost island’ is meant to show that

options.text: if Anselm’s form of argument worked, we could prove a greatest conceivable island exists — which we should not grant

questions.explanation: The parody tests whether the formula applies uniquely to God or licenses any ‘greatest F’.

questions.prompt: Anselm’s reply, in spirit, is that

options.text: ‘that than which nothing greater can be thought’ is not a contingent greatest-of-a-kind the way an island is — the fool already has God in intellect in a different way

questions.explanation: You may still side with Gaunilo. The sitting is whether the formula is unique, not whether you like islands.

questions.prompt: A good student mistake is to think Gaunilo

options.text: denies that we can think of a lost island
simply hasn’t read the Proslogion’s words, rather than offering a structural objection
uses a parody of the form

questions.explanation: He has read them. The objection is that the form proves too much.

units.title: Philosophy under the Law
units.professorNote: These two sit here because they enter the Latin conversation about faith and reason — not as a tour of Islamic and Jewish thought for its own sake (that would be another course).

assignments.title: Averroes: the Law and demonstration
assignments.author: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
assignments.work: Decisive Discourse on the Relation between Religion and Philosophy
assignments.why: Does the Law command, permit, or forbid the study of philosophy? Averroes argues that demonstration is required for those able, and that truth cannot contradict truth: when scripture seems to conflict with demonstration, the apparent sense is to be interpreted. Latin ‘Averroism’ will later be a scare-word for double truth. Read him first as trying to prevent that split.
lookFor: The legal question: is philosophizing obligatory for some?
‘Truth does not contradict truth’ as a rule of interpretation
Different classes of people, different methods (rhetoric, dialectic, demonstration)
questions: Is this harmony, or a ranking that makes philosophy the judge of scripture’s sense?
What danger is he trying to save the community from?
assignments.nextHint: Maimonides: how not to speak of God as if God were a magnified creature.

quiz.title: After the Decisive Treatise
quiz.intro: Law and demonstration as two addresses, not two truths as a slogan.

questions.prompt: Averroes’s practical claim about philosophy and the Law is that

options.text: philosophy is forbidden to all Muslims
demonstration is a religious duty for those capable of it, and the Law has a rhetorical/poetic address for others
the Quran has no inner sense
Aristotle is a prophet in the legal sense

questions.explanation: The sitting: who may allegorize, and why apparent conflict is not a license for the untrained to discard the Law.

questions.prompt: When demonstration and the apparent sense of scripture seem to clash, Averroes’s trained reader

options.text: interprets the apparent sense, because truth does not contradict truth

questions.explanation: That is the harmony thesis in this treatise — not a cheap ‘double truth’ meme unless you find it in the pages.

questions.prompt: The Decisive Treatise argues that every believer must study the Physics.
questions.explanation: The point is differential address: demonstration is not for every audience.

assignments.title: Maimonides: attributes and perplexity
assignments.author: Maimonides
assignments.why: The Guide is for someone torn between the Law and the philosophers. The attribute chapters teach a discipline: many predicates said of God cannot be real accidents in God. Negative theology — saying what God is not — is a way of protecting both unity and speech. Aquinas will borrow and recast this. Read for the problem of religious language, not for a complete Maimonidean system.
lookFor: Who the ‘perplexed’ reader is
Why positive attributes threaten divine simplicity
What remains of God-talk if many names are negations or relations
questions: Is negative theology still knowledge of God, or a rule for silence?
How would Anselm’s ‘greater’ have to be rewritten under this discipline?
assignments.nextHint: Aquinas: sacred doctrine, the Five Ways, natural law.

quiz.title: After Guide I.50–52 (and the assigned stretch)
quiz.intro: Attributes, and what we may not say of God.

questions.prompt: In this stretch, Maimonides is especially concerned to

options.text: block univocal positive attributes that would make God composite or like creatures
prove the Five Ways in Aquinas’s later numbering

questions.explanation: The sitting: negative theology as a philosophical-religious discipline, not a vibe.

questions.prompt: Equivocation on names of God matters because

options.text: if ‘knows’ or ‘lives’ meant the same in God and in us, we would have imported creaturely structure into the divine

questions.explanation: Look for the argument about attribution, not a biography of Maimonides.

questions.prompt: These chapters teach that ordinary praise of God is always philosophically sufficient as it stands.
questions.explanation: The Guide’s pressure is that unexamined speech is a theological error.

units.title: Aquinas: demonstration, God, law
units.professorNote: Three short scholastic sittings. Learn the form (objections, sed contra, respondeo) as a way of thinking, not as a relic.

assignments.title: Summa I q.1: whether sacred doctrine is a science
assignments.author: Thomas Aquinas
assignments.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
assignments.why: Is theology a science? Does it need philosophy? Can it prove God, or only take God on authority? Question 1 is the methods sitting: sacred doctrine as a science that takes its principles from a higher knowledge (God’s), and that can still use philosophy as a handmaid. This is how Aquinas will refuse both ‘fideism’ and ‘philosophy as rival church.’
lookFor: The article-form: objections, sed contra, corpus, replies
Sacred doctrine as a science whose principles are received
How philosophy is used without being the source of those principles
questions: If the principles are revealed, in what sense is this still scientia?
Where would Averroes and Aquinas agree about demonstration, and where not?
assignments.nextHint: Question 2: whether God exists, and the Five Ways.

quiz.title: After ST I q.1
quiz.intro: Why a ‘science’ of revelation.

questions.prompt: Sacred doctrine is called a science, in q.1, because

options.text: it uses no premises from revelation
it proceeds from principles known by the light of a higher science (God’s knowledge / revelation), as subaltern sciences do

questions.explanation: The sitting: how theology can be a scientia without being a first philosophy that proves its own highest principles.

questions.prompt: Philosophy is not useless here because

options.text: natural reason can demonstrate some preambles and can serve sacred doctrine without replacing it
only the Five Ways count as philosophy

questions.explanation: q.1 sets the relation of the two lights before q.2’s ways.

questions.prompt: Question 1 claims that sacred doctrine is unnecessary if one has the Physics.
questions.explanation: Revelation is needed for an end that exceeds natural reason — that is the opening argument.

assignments.title: Summa I q.2: the Five Ways
assignments.author: Thomas Aquinas
assignments.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
assignments.selection: Prima pars, question 2 (especially a.3, the Five Ways)
assignments.why: God’s existence is not self-evident to us (Anselm is refused). It can be demonstrated from effects. The Five Ways: motion, efficient cause, contingency, degrees, governance. Each is short. Each depends on a picture of explanation you have from Aristotle: no infinite regress in ordered causes, actuality before potentiality. Do not memorize nicknames. Reconstruct one way slowly.
lookFor: Why the ontological argument is set aside in a.1–2
The shared shape: from observed features to a first that we call God
What ‘and this we call God’ is doing — naming, not yet describing the Trinity
questions: Pick one Way. Where is the most disputable premise?
Does ‘first mover’ already smuggle in a theistic God, or only a terminus of explanation?
assignments.nextHint: Natural law: how reason in us participates in eternal law.

quiz.title: After ST I q.2
quiz.intro: Five ways, not one slogan.

questions.prompt: Each ‘way’ is, structurally,

options.text: a proof from scripture quotation alone
a movement from observed features of the world (motion, causation, contingency, degrees, governance) to a first that all call God

questions.explanation: You were asked to state at least one way with its middle term, not to chant ‘first cause.’

questions.prompt: The ways, as Aquinas frames them, conclude to

options.text: a first source to which the name God is given — not yet the whole of Christian doctrine

questions.explanation: A common misreading inflates q.2 into the Summa. It is a metaphysical approach to ‘whether God exists.’

questions.prompt: A student who says ‘science refuted the first way’ without stating the first way has

options.text: skipped the sitting: you must first hear motion as reduction from potency, and a first mover as Aquinas argues it

questions.explanation: LookFor was the argument’s steps, not a newspaper headline.

questions.prompt: The Five Ways are five versions of Anselm’s ontological argument.
questions.explanation: They start from the world (a posteriori), not from the concept of that-than-which.

assignments.title: Summa I–II qq.90, 94: law and the natural law
assignments.author: Thomas Aquinas
assignments.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
assignments.selection: I–II q.90 (essence of law) and q.94 (natural law)
assignments.why: Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by who has care of the community, and promulgated. Natural law is the rational creature’s participation in eternal law — its first precept: good is to be done and pursued, evil avoided. This is the ancestor of later rights talk and of every fight about whether nature grounds ethics. Hume and Moore will try to break the move from is to ought. Remember where the move was built.
lookFor: The four notes of law in q.90
Eternal, natural, human, divine law as a hierarchy
The first precept of natural law and how other precepts are said to follow
questions: Is ‘good is to be done’ a tautology, a perception, or a command?
What would it take for human law to fail as law, on this account?
assignments.nextHint: The early modern break: Bacon against idols, Descartes against the whole inherited edifice.

quiz.title: After ST I–II qq.90 and 94
quiz.intro: Law’s definition, and the precepts of practical reason.

questions.prompt: Law, in q.90, is

options.text: an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated

questions.explanation: Four notes. Missing any one (especially reason and common good) is a misreading of ‘law’ here.

questions.prompt: The first precept of natural law in q.94 is

options.text: good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided — with natural inclinations specifying goods (life, knowledge, social life, etc.)
there is no natural law, only command

questions.explanation: The sitting: synderesis / first practical principles, not a complete modern rights list.

questions.prompt: Natural law can fail to be known in particular cases, on this account, because

options.text: passion, vice, and custom can obscure conclusions even if the first precept is not abolished
only the sovereign creates all morality

questions.explanation: q.94’s discussion of change and ignorance is part of the doctrine, not a later footnote.

recapQuiz.title: Aquinas: recap
recapQuiz.intro: A science of revelation, five ways from the world, and practical reason’s first precepts.

questions.prompt: Sacred doctrine is a science, in q.1, because it

options.text: subalternates to a higher knowledge, as other sciences take principles from a superior

questions.explanation: q.1 is the relation of two lights, before q.2.

questions.prompt: The Five Ways are

options.text: a posteriori paths from features of the world to a first that is called God

questions.explanation: Do not inflate q.2 into the whole Summa.

questions.prompt: Natural law’s first precept is

options.text: good is to be done and pursued, evil avoided — specified via natural inclinations

questions.explanation: q.90’s definition of law (reason, common good, competent maker, promulgation) frames q.94.

questions.prompt: Aquinas thinks particular conclusions of natural law can never be obscured by vice or custom.
questions.explanation: q.94 discusses just that obscuring. The first precept is not a complete code in every mind.

questions.prompt: This unit’s order (doctrine, ways, law) teaches that

options.text: metaphysical theology and practical reason are distinct sittings of one system

questions.explanation: You need q.1 to know what q.2 is doing, and both to hear law as ordinance of reason.

eras.title: The early modern break
eras.intro: Authority as a way of knowing comes under suspicion. Bacon catalogues the idols that distort inquiry; Descartes rebuilds from the cogito; Spinoza identifies God with Nature; Pascal wagers in the dark; Leibniz fills the world with windowless monads. You are watching metaphysics try to become as certain as geometry — and watching that ambition split.

units.title: Idols and method
units.professorNote: Bacon for the diagnosis of error; Descartes’ Discourse for the autobiography of a method. Then the Meditations, split.

assignments.title: Novum Organum I: the idols
assignments.author: Francis Bacon
assignments.selection: Book I aphorisms, especially the four idols
assignments.pages: Novum Organum Book I (idols of Tribe, Cave, Marketplace, Theatre)
assignments.why: Before a new organon, the mind’s built-in distortions must be named. Tribe (human nature), Cave (the individual den), Marketplace (words), Theatre (received systems). This is not yet Hume on custom. It is a call to discipline attention toward nature by experiment and tables of instances. Read the idols as a theory of error you can still use on yourself.
lookFor: The four idols, with one example each that is not Bacon’s own
Why words (Marketplace) can fail even when speakers are sincere
What ‘Theatre’ implies about Aristotle and the schools
questions: Is Bacon’s remedy a method you could state in steps, or a temperament?
Which idol would he say is most active when you quote a famous philosopher instead of looking?
assignments.nextHint: Descartes will try to make method a sequence you can follow from the armchair — then from the stove-heated room.

quiz.title: After Novum Organum I (idols)
quiz.intro: Four idols, as a discipline of the mind.

questions.prompt: Bacon’s idols are

options.text: systematic prejudices of the tribe, cave, marketplace, and theatre that block a new induction
the four causes under new names

questions.explanation: The sitting: diagnosis before method. Idols of the theatre include received philosophical systems.

questions.prompt: Idols of the marketplace especially concern

options.text: the deceit of words — names that muddle inquiry
the human species’ senses as such

questions.explanation: Tribe (human nature), cave (individual), marketplace (language), theatre (doctrine) — keep them distinct.

questions.prompt: Bacon’s aim in this stretch is to defend scholastic disputation as the organon of the sciences.
questions.explanation: Novum Organum is a replacement organon. The idols explain why the old one fails.

assignments.title: Discourse on the Method, Parts I–IV
assignments.author: René Descartes
assignments.selection: Parts I–IV (hosted file: Parts II–IV; read those as the method, morals, and cogito)
assignments.pages: Discourse Parts II–IV (Veitch); Part I if your edition has it
assignments.why: The Discourse is the public story: reject what is only probable, follow rules of method, a provisional morality, then the cogito and God as the rescue of certainty. It is easier than the Meditations and slightly more dangerous, because it sounds like a life-hack. It is not. It is a claim about what knowledge requires.
lookFor: The rules of method (Part II)
Why a provisional morality is needed while tearing down the house
The cogito as it appears here, before the full skeptical machinery
questions: What survives if you refuse his rules but keep his demand for certainty?
Is the provisional morality a confession that method cannot guide life, or a temporary scaffold?
assignments.nextHint: Meditations I–II: doubt, then the ‘I’ that doubts.

quiz.title: After Discourse on the Method (assigned parts)
quiz.intro: Method, morale, and a first sketch of the ‘I’.

questions.prompt: The method’s rules (Part 2) emphasize

options.text: evidence, division of difficulties, order, and complete enumerations

questions.explanation: The sitting is the rules as a discipline, not a biography of the stove.

questions.prompt: The provisional morale (Part 3) is there because

options.text: Descartes has already rebuilt all science
one must live while the house of belief is under renovation — a temporary ethics of moderation and resolution

questions.explanation: Do not confuse the morale with the later metaphysics. It is a scaffold.

questions.prompt: Part 4’s ‘I think’ sketch is

options.text: a full physics of the heart
a first publication of the cogito and a proof of God and the soul’s distinction — tighter in the Meditations

questions.explanation: The Discourse is a public narrative; the Meditations will slow the same moves down.

units.title: The Meditations, in three sittings
units.professorNote: Do not read all six in one night. The splits follow the argument’s joints.

assignments.title: Meditations I–II: doubt and the thinking thing
assignments.author: René Descartes
assignments.pages: Meditation I (things doubtful); Meditation II (the nature of the mind)
assignments.why: First sitting: the demolition. Senses, dreaming, the malicious deceiver. Then: if I am deceived, I am. The ‘I’ is a thinking thing, known more distinctly than the wax is known by the senses. The wax is not a detour; it shows what the intellect does when the sensible qualities change. Molyneux’s English is seventeenth-century and public domain. Slow down for the archaism; the argument is the same.
lookFor: Each stage of doubt and what it still leaves standing
Why the cogito is not an inference from a general premise, as he presents it
The wax: what remains, and by what faculty it is known
questions: Does the dreaming argument undermine all sensory belief, or only some?
Is ‘I am a thinking thing’ a discovery of a substance, or only of an activity?
assignments.nextHint: III–IV: God, and why error does not refute clear and distinct perception.

quiz.title: After Meditations I–II
quiz.intro: Doubt as an instrument, and the cogito.

questions.prompt: The dreaming and deceiver hypotheses are meant to

options.text: withdraw assent from all that can be doubted, including the senses and even mathematical belief under a powerful deceiver

questions.explanation: Methodic doubt is not a lifestyle. It is a filter for what is certain.

questions.prompt: ‘I am, I exist’ survives because

options.text: even if I am deceived, I who am deceived must be — thought is the attribute I cannot separate from myself here
Aristotle defined the soul as this

questions.explanation: The sitting: what I am, at this stage, is a thinking thing — not yet a proof of the body’s existence.

questions.prompt: The wax example shows that

options.text: the nature of the wax is grasped by the mind, not by the changing sensory appearances

questions.explanation: It is an argument about intellect’s grasp of body, still inside Meditation II’s thin ontology.

questions.prompt: By the end of Meditation II, Descartes has proved that other human bodies exist.
questions.explanation: The external world waits. II secures the ‘I’ and a first account of mind.

assignments.title: Meditations III–IV: God and error
assignments.author: René Descartes
assignments.pages: Meditation III (God); Meditation IV (truth and falsity)
assignments.why: The idea of an infinite God cannot have come from a finite mind, he claims; God exists and is not a deceiver. Then: error comes from the will outrunning the intellect. This is the rescue of ‘clear and distinct’ from the evil genius — and the notorious circle if God’s guarantee is proved by perceptions that only God could guarantee. Name the circle even if you think there is a way out.
lookFor: The causal principle about ideas and their objective reality
Why God cannot be a deceiver, on his telling
Will vs intellect as the account of error
questions: State the Cartesian circle in one careful sentence.
Could a finite mind invent the idea of the infinite by negation, as some objectors said?
assignments.nextHint: V–VI: essence of matter, existence of bodies, real distinction of mind and body.

quiz.title: After Meditations III–IV
quiz.intro: God as guarantor, and the source of error.

questions.prompt: The idea of God in III is used to argue that

options.text: a finite substance could not be the total cause of the idea of an infinite perfect being — so God exists as cause
the evil genius has already won

questions.explanation: Causal adequacy of ideas is the engine. You may reject it; you must state it.

questions.prompt: Meditation IV locates error in

options.text: the will’s outrunning the intellect — judging beyond what is clearly and distinctly perceived

questions.explanation: Theodicy of error: God is not a deceiver; misuse of freedom explains falsity.

questions.prompt: A clear and distinct perception, for Descartes here, may still be false if God is no deceiver.
questions.explanation: The divine guarantee is what makes C&D the rule of truth — that is the circularity worry you were asked to feel.

assignments.title: Meditations V–VI: essence, bodies, dualism
assignments.author: René Descartes
assignments.pages: Meditation V (essence of material things; God again); Meditation VI (existence of bodies; mind–body distinction)
assignments.why: A second ontological argument appears; then the essence of matter as extension. Meditation VI restores the world — not by naive trust in the senses, but by a God who would deceive us if the strong inclination to believe in bodies had no object. Mind and body are really distinct because each can be conceived clearly without the other. The union remains a fact of sensation and confusion. Spinoza will refuse the two-substance picture.
lookFor: Matter as extension — what is being excluded (weight, color as intrinsic)
The argument for the existence of bodies
Real distinction of mind and body, and the leftover problem of their union
questions: If mind is better known than body, why do we still say we have a body?
What would have to be true for this dualism to make a living animal unintelligible?
assignments.nextHint: Spinoza: one substance, God-or-Nature.

quiz.title: After Meditations V–VI
quiz.intro: Essence of matter, God again, and the union.

questions.prompt: Meditation V’s ontological argument claims that

options.text: existence is never contained in an essence
existence belongs to God’s essence as a mountain’s valley belongs to the mountain — God cannot be thought as not existing

questions.explanation: A second theistic proof, from essence. Compare with III without collapsing them.

questions.prompt: Meditation VI argues that

options.text: the mind is a mode of body
body exists, mind and body are really distinct, yet I am a union — sensation teaches the composite
other minds are known by the cogito alone

questions.explanation: The sitting: dualism plus embodied life. Neither slogan (‘only mind’ / ‘only machine’) is the whole of VI.

questions.prompt: The real distinction of mind and body is argued from

options.text: clearly conceiving one without the other, given God’s power to bring about what is clearly conceived

questions.explanation: That is the modal argument for dualism. Keep it distinct from the union’s phenomenology.

recapQuiz.title: Meditations: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Doubt, God, error, essence, and the union — one arc, three sittings.

questions.prompt: Meditations I–II secure

options.text: the thinking I, after a doubt that includes dreaming and a deceiver

questions.explanation: Wax is about mind’s grasp, still inside a thin ontology.

questions.prompt: III–IV add

options.text: God as cause of the idea of the infinite, and error as the will’s overreach

questions.explanation: The circularity worry (C&D guaranteed by a God proved using C&D) belongs here.

questions.prompt: V–VI add

options.text: an ontological argument, the real distinction of mind and body, and the composite of sensation
Spinoza’s one substance as Descartes’ conclusion

questions.explanation: Dualism plus union: neither slogan is the whole of VI.

questions.prompt: The Discourse’s provisional morale is the same sitting as Meditation VI’s union.
questions.explanation: The Discourse was a scaffold for living; the Meditations slow the metaphysics. Different assignments.

questions.prompt: A mistake this unit is designed to kill is that methodic doubt is

options.text: a recommendation to live as a skeptic
compatible with a later divine guarantee

questions.explanation: Doubt is a filter, not a lifestyle. Hume will later refuse this rebuild.

units.title: God-or-Nature, the wager, monads
units.professorNote: Three alternatives to Cartesian two-substance theism. None is a footnote.

assignments.title: Ethics I: God or Nature
assignments.author: Baruch Spinoza
assignments.selection: Part I, through the appendix if your sitting includes it
assignments.pages: Ethics Part I (definitions, axioms, key propositions on substance and God)
assignments.why: One substance, God-or-Nature, infinite attributes. Finite things are modes. Nothing is contingent. The geometric form is not decoration: he thinks this can be demonstrated. The appendix against final causes is the ethical payoff of the metaphysics. Read slowly. One sitting cannot master Part I; it can show you the claim that Descartes’ two created substances cannot stand.
lookFor: Definitions of substance, attribute, mode
Why there cannot be two substances of the same nature
The denial of final causes in the appendix (if present in your stretch)
questions: Is this pantheism, atheism, or a third thing Spinoza would not name that way?
What happens to prayer, miracle, and free will if Part I is true?
assignments.nextHint: Pascal: the heart, wretchedness, and the wager — a different use of uncertainty.

quiz.title: After Ethics Part I
quiz.intro: God or Nature, and the affect of necessity.

questions.prompt: For Spinoza in Part I, substance is

options.text: created by a person-like God from nothing each day
that which is in itself and conceived through itself — and there is only one, God or Nature, with infinite attributes

questions.explanation: Deus sive Natura. Finite things are modes, not rival substances.

questions.prompt: Nothing is contingent, on this account, because

options.text: everything follows from the necessity of the divine nature; ‘could have been otherwise’ is a defect of our imagination
only humans are free in Descartes’ sense
Aristotle’s chance is the highest cause

questions.explanation: The sitting: necessity as metaphysics, not a mood of fatalism as popularly pictured.

questions.prompt: Part I treats God as a lawgiver who might have made a different world by arbitrary will.
questions.explanation: Will and intellect in God are not a king’s choices. That is the anti-creation-as-decree move.

assignments.title: Pascal: wretchedness and the wager
assignments.author: Blaise Pascal
assignments.selection: The hosted cluster on diversion, wretchedness, and the wager
assignments.pages: Pensées (Trotter): the wager sitting as hosted
assignments.why: Reason cannot settle God; the wager asks you to treat belief as a decision under uncertainty with infinite stake. Around it: we run to diversion because we cannot sit quietly in a room; greatness and wretchedness together. This is not Aquinas’s demonstration. It is a psychology of the betting animal. You may hate the wager and still need its picture of the human.
lookFor: Why diversion (divertissement) is a philosophical clue, not a moralizing aside
The structure of the wager: what is staked, what is gained
What the wager does not claim to prove
questions: Does the wager require that you can choose belief?
Is an infinite prize enough to make any finite risk rational — and what does ‘rational’ mean here?
assignments.nextHint: Leibniz: a world of monads instead of one substance or two.

quiz.title: After the Wager (and assigned Pensées)
quiz.intro: Reason’s limits, and a practical argument.

questions.prompt: The Wager argues that

options.text: God’s existence is demonstrated like a triangle
if you must wager, the expected value of living as if God exists dominates, given infinite gain

questions.explanation: It is a practical argument under uncertainty, not a fifth Way.

questions.prompt: A limit Pascal insists on is that

options.text: geometry can prove the God of Abraham
the heart has reasons, and the philosophical God is not yet the God of the patriarchs — the Wager sits inside that humility

questions.explanation: The sitting: do not inflate the Wager into the whole of the Pensées, but do hear why it is not a theorem.

questions.prompt: Pascal thinks the Wager replaces the need to live a religious life after deciding.
questions.explanation: Custom, mass, and habituation are part of how one comes to believe — the fragment’s own continuation.

assignments.title: The Monadology
assignments.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
assignments.why: Simple substances without windows, mirroring the universe from a point of view; pre-established harmony instead of Descartes’ pineal traffic. This is a complete metaphysical picture in a pamphlet. You will not ‘get’ every scholium. Get: why composites need simples, why monads cannot interact, how God chooses the best of possible worlds.
lookFor: Why a monad has no windows (no genuine influx)
Perception and apperception — not all monads are minds like ours
Pre-established harmony as an alternative to occasionalism and to physical influx
questions: Is the best-possible-world claim a theodicy you can test, or a consequence of God’s definition?
How does this answer Spinoza’s one-substance claim without returning to Descartes’ two?
assignments.nextHint: Empiricism will ask how any of these systems could be known from experience.

quiz.title: After the Monadology
quiz.intro: Windowless simples, and a pre-established harmony.

questions.prompt: A monad is

options.text: a simple, windowless substance whose inner states unfold from its complete concept — perception and appetition, not parts
a mode of Spinoza’s one substance only, with no plurality of substances

questions.explanation: Simples without windows: no causal influx of accidents from outside.

questions.prompt: Pre-established harmony is Leibniz’s way of saying that

options.text: mind and body (and monads generally) agree because God created a world of substances whose programs correspond — not because they transduce force into thought

questions.explanation: The sitting: a reply to Descartes’ union problem and to occasionalism, in a sentence.

questions.prompt: This is ‘the best of possible worlds’ because

options.text: God chooses the world with the greatest variety/order among possibles — evil is permitted under that optimization, not as a first good
monads can see out their windows after all

questions.explanation: A theodicy, not a cheer. Voltaire’s later joke is not the text.

questions.prompt: Monads have physical windows through which accidents migrate.
questions.explanation: ‘Windowless’ is the technical refusal of influx.

recapQuiz.title: After Descartes: recap
recapQuiz.intro: One substance, a wager, and windowless simples — three replies.

questions.prompt: Spinoza’s God-or-Nature, relative to Descartes, is a refusal of

options.text: created finite substances and a lawgiving will that could have done otherwise

questions.explanation: Modes, not rival substances. Necessity is the affect of Part I.

questions.prompt: Pascal’s Wager is

options.text: a practical argument under uncertainty, inside a humility about the God of the philosophers vs Abraham

questions.explanation: Do not inflate it into the whole of the Pensées, but do not treat it as a theorem either.

questions.prompt: Leibniz’s monads and harmony are a reply to

options.text: the mind–body union problem (and occasionalism) without influx through ‘windows’

questions.explanation: Best possible world is a theodicy of optimization, not a cheer.

questions.prompt: These three authors agree that finite minds are modes of one substance.
questions.explanation: Only Spinoza says that. Leibniz multiplies substances; Pascal is not doing Ethics I.

questions.prompt: The unit’s pedagogical point is that

options.text: the Meditations’ dualism and theodicy of error immediately generate rival systems

questions.explanation: Hobbes and Locke come next as a different pressure: bodies, experience, politics.

eras.title: Empiricism and the new science
eras.intro: If all knowledge comes from experience, what happens to innate ideas, substance, causation, the self, and God? Hobbes builds a politics from bodies in motion; Locke fills the blank slate and then a theory of property and consent; Berkeley removes matter; Hume wakes Kant. This era is the pressure test of Descartes’ rationalism.

units.title: Bodies, fear, and property
units.professorNote: Hobbes and Locke disagree about the state of nature and about what a sovereign is for. Read them as a pair.

assignments.title: Leviathan 13–14: the natural condition
assignments.author: Thomas Hobbes
assignments.why: Without a common power, life is a war of all against all — not because people are cartoon villains, but because equality of vulnerability plus the right of nature (to everything needful for life) makes preemptive violence rational. The first two natural laws: seek peace; be willing to lay down liberty when others do, in a contract. This is Machiavelli’s honesty turned into a science of bodies.
lookFor: Why equality, not monstrous vice, drives the war
The right of nature versus the law of nature
What a covenant is, and why it needs a sword
questions: Is the state of nature a history, a thought experiment, or a warning about civil war?
Can there be injustice before a sovereign, on this account?
assignments.nextHint: Chapters 17–21: the generation of the commonwealth and the liberty that remains.

quiz.title: After Leviathan 13–14
quiz.intro: War from equality, not from cartoon vice.

questions.prompt: Hobbes’s war of all against all is driven, in these chapters, mainly by

options.text: equality of vulnerability plus the right of nature to what one judges needful — which makes preemption rational

questions.explanation: LookFor: equality, not vice, as the engine. Competition, diffidence, glory are the three causes of quarrel.

questions.prompt: The right of nature differs from a law of nature in that

options.text: right is liberty to use power; law is a precept that binds (seek peace; be willing to lay down right when others do)
law exists only after a sovereign, so chapter 14 cannot mention it

questions.explanation: Injustice as breaking covenant waits on a power to enforce. The laws of nature are still precepts of reason in 14.

questions.prompt: A covenant, here, needs a sword because

options.text: words alone do not bind where there is no common power to punish — covenants without the sword are but words
the state of nature already has courts

questions.explanation: That is why the sitting points to chapters 17–21 next.

questions.prompt: On this account there can already be injustice, in the full civil sense, before a sovereign.
questions.explanation: Where there is no common power, there is no law in the sense that makes injury a crime. That is Hobbes’s sting.

assignments.title: Leviathan 17–21: the mortal god
assignments.author: Thomas Hobbes
assignments.pages: Leviathan chs. 17–18, 21 (18 is in the hosted stretch toward 21)
assignments.why: The commonwealth is generated when authorization creates an artificial person. The sovereign is not a party to the covenant in the way subjects are. Liberty of subjects is the silence of the law — and the inalienable right to defend one’s life. Locke will deny that you can consent to arbitrary power. Keep Hobbes’s claim sharp so the denial has an object.
lookFor: Authorization and the artificial person
Why the sovereign is not bound as a fellow covenanter
The remaining liberty: self-defense, and gaps in law
questions: Is this absolutism, or a theory of the minimum conditions of peace?
Where does Hobbes leave room, if any, for resistance?
assignments.nextHint: Locke: property in the state of nature, before government.

quiz.title: After Leviathan 17–18 and 21
quiz.intro: Authorization, and the liberty that remains.

questions.prompt: The commonwealth is generated when

options.text: each authorizes one person or assembly to bear their person — a real unity, not a mere crowd
the Church crowns a king only

questions.explanation: Authorization and representation are the legal-metaphysical move, not only fear.

questions.prompt: The sovereign’s rights, in ch. 18, include that subjects

options.text: may lawfully split sovereignty whenever they dislike a tax
cannot accuse the sovereign of injustice in the covenant’s terms — they have authorized the acts
retain a private right to all things as in ch. 13

questions.explanation: A common misreading is ‘might makes right’ without the authorization story.

questions.prompt: True liberty of subjects in ch. 21 is, for Hobbes,

options.text: a natural right to everything remaining after the covenant
the silence of the law — plus the inalienable right to defend one’s life
democratic participation as a natural right
the right to abolish the sovereign at will without contradiction

questions.explanation: The sitting: what liberty remains. It is not a liberal bill of rights avant la lettre.

assignments.title: Second Treatise V: property
assignments.author: John Locke
assignments.selection: Chapter V, with II (state of nature) as frame; glance at XIX on dissolution
assignments.pages: Second Treatise chs. II, V, and XIX as hosted
assignments.why: The state of nature already has law (reason), not Hobbes’s war. Property begins in the person, then in mixing labor with what is common, limited by spoilage and enough-and-as-good. Money later relaxes the spoilage limit — a hinge many readers miss. Chapter XIX: government dissolves when it betrays trust. This is the ancestor of liberal revolution and of later critiques of accumulation.
lookFor: Labor-mixing as a title, and the two provisos
What money does to the original limits
Dissolution versus Hobbesian authorization that cannot be withdrawn
questions: Does ‘enough and as good’ still hold after money?
What makes Locke’s state of nature not already a government?
assignments.nextHint: Now Locke’s Essay: where ideas come from.

quiz.title: After Second Treatise (assigned chapters)
quiz.intro: Labor, consent, and when government dissolves.

questions.prompt: Property in the state of nature, for Locke, begins in

options.text: mixing labor with what is common, within the spoilage limit and (later) the invention of money
inheritance from Adam as Filmer has it, without labor

questions.explanation: Ch. 5 is the labor theory and its provisos. Do not skip the limits.

questions.prompt: Political society is made by

options.text: consent to form a community that may then use majority to settle the government — not tacit remaining under a conqueror as if that were enough
divine right of kings as the only title
the war of all against all as Hobbes describes it, without remainder

questions.explanation: Ch. 8: consent. Compare Hobbes: Locke’s natural condition already has law of nature and property.

questions.prompt: Government may be dissolved, in the assigned later chapter, when

options.text: it acts contrary to the trust — tyranny as exercise of power beyond right

questions.explanation: Ch. 19: appeal to heaven is not a weekly hobby. It is the right of resistance when trust is broken.

questions.prompt: Locke’s state of nature is identical with Hobbes’s war of all against all.
questions.explanation: Locke has a law of nature and property before the magistrate. That is the disagreement the unit is for.

recapQuiz.title: Hobbes and Locke: recap
recapQuiz.intro: War, authorization, labor, and trust.

questions.prompt: Hobbes’s natural condition is a war chiefly because of

options.text: equality of vulnerability and a right to all that makes preemption rational

questions.explanation: Chs. 13–14. Injustice as crime waits on a sword.

questions.prompt: Locke’s natural condition already includes

options.text: no property and no law of nature
a law of nature and property by labor, before the magistrate
authorization of an unlimited sovereign as the first act

questions.explanation: That is why the unit is a disagreement, not a sequel.

questions.prompt: Hobbesian liberty of subjects is mainly

options.text: a natural right to everything remaining
the silence of the law, plus defense of life
a right of revolution whenever taxes exist

questions.explanation: Ch. 21. Locke’s ch. 19 is a different account of dissolution.

questions.prompt: Locke treats conquest as a complete title equivalent to consent.
questions.explanation: Consent (and trust) are the titles. Tyranny is power beyond right.

questions.prompt: Authorization (Hobbes) vs trust (Locke) names

options.text: whether the sovereign’s acts are yours by representation, or limited by a fiduciary end

questions.explanation: Keep the two political metaphysics distinct before Hume and Rousseau.

units.title: Ideas, qualities, minds
units.professorNote: Locke’s epistemology, then Berkeley’s shock. Hume will finish the demolition of necessary connection.

assignments.title: Essay I: against innate principles
assignments.author: John Locke
assignments.pages: Essay Book I (hosted: I.2 onward in the file’s sections)
assignments.why: No innate speculative or practical principles. Universal consent is a bad test, and children and ‘idiots’ are a better one. The mind begins as white paper. This is the charter of British empiricism. Descartes’ innate idea of God is in the dock.
lookFor: Why universal consent would not prove innateness even if it existed
The appeal to those who have not learned the supposed maxims
What ‘white paper’ does and does not mean (not: no faculties)
questions: Could a disposition to form an idea be innate even if the idea is not?
What happens to morality if there are no innate practical principles?
assignments.nextHint: Book II: simple ideas, and primary vs secondary qualities.

quiz.title: After Essay I.2 (and the assigned anti-innatism)
quiz.intro: The blank paper is an argument, not a metaphor only.

questions.prompt: Locke attacks innate speculative principles because

options.text: there is no universal consent, and what is later agreed can be explained by teaching and reason — so innateness is idle

questions.explanation: LookFor: no universal consent; learning explains apparent innateness.

questions.prompt: ‘Innate’ would be a useful hypothesis, on his terms, only if

options.text: the mark were actually in all minds independently of instruction — which he denies we find

questions.explanation: The sitting is the argumentative burden, not a slogan ‘empiricism.’

questions.prompt: Locke thinks we are born with the idea of God stamped on the mind as a letter is stamped on paper.
questions.explanation: That is the view I.2 is written against. God is known another way, later in the Essay.

assignments.title: Essay II.8: primary and secondary qualities
assignments.author: John Locke
assignments.selection: Book II, ch. 8 (and enough of II.1 to see sensation and reflection)
assignments.why: Ideas come from sensation and reflection. Primary qualities (bulk, figure, motion) are in bodies; secondary (color, sound, taste) are powers to produce ideas in us. This is the corpuscular world meeting the mind. Berkeley will say the distinction cannot be maintained. Get Locke’s distinction clean before the attack.
lookFor: Sensation vs reflection as the two fountains
Primary qualities as inseparable from body
Secondary qualities as powers — not nothing, but not ‘in the object’ as yellow is in the idea
questions: If color is a power, is the world colorless when unobserved, on Locke’s view?
What problem about resemblance (idea resembling quality) is already visible?
assignments.nextHint: Berkeley: to be is to be perceived.

quiz.title: After Essay II.1, 8, 27 (assigned)
quiz.intro: Ideas from experience; primary/secondary; personal identity.

questions.prompt: All ideas, for Locke here, come from

options.text: sensation and reflection — experience in two directions

questions.explanation: II.1: the fountain. Simple ideas are not made by us at will.

questions.prompt: Secondary qualities are

options.text: in the object just as we sense them, independently of us
powers in bodies to produce sensations (color, taste) that are not resemblances of the body’s bulk, figure, motion

questions.explanation: II.8: the distinction. A common mistake is to think Locke denies that objects cause color-experience.

questions.prompt: Personal identity, in II.27, is

options.text: sameness of soul-substance as such, always
sameness of consciousness — a forensic notion for reward and punishment

questions.explanation: The sitting: consciousness, not a hidden substance, as the person. Thought-experiments of transfer are the method.

assignments.title: Berkeley: Principles, opening
assignments.author: George Berkeley
assignments.work: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
assignments.pages: Principles, Introduction and opening sections (as hosted)
assignments.why: Abstract general ideas are a Lockean fiction that makes skepticism inevitable. Ordinary objects are collections of ideas. Matter as an unthinking substance behind ideas is unnecessary and unintelligible. God sustains the order of ideas. This is not ‘everything is a dream.’ It is an attempt to save common sense and science without material substance.
lookFor: The attack on abstract general ideas
What an apple is, if it is a collection of ideas
Why matter is said to do no explanatory work
questions: Does Berkeley abolish the external world, or only a philosopher’s extra object?
What role must God play if ideas persist when you leave the room?
assignments.nextHint: Hume: causation as custom, not insight into necessity.

quiz.title: After the Principles (introduction and opening)
quiz.intro: To be is to be perceived — as an argument.

questions.prompt: Berkeley’s attack on abstract general ideas (introduction) claims that

options.text: we cannot form the idea of a triangle that is neither equilateral nor scalene, etc. — abstraction as Locke describes it is a fiction

questions.explanation: The introduction is not optional. It undercuts a certain theory of meaning before the ontology.

questions.prompt: ‘Esse is percipi’ for unthinking things means

options.text: their being is to be perceived (or to perceive, in the case of spirits); matter as inert substratum is idle
only my mind exists (solipsism as his conclusion)

questions.explanation: He keeps God and other spirits. Idealism here is not ‘only I exist.’

questions.prompt: Berkeley thinks the laws of nature cannot be stated because there are no bodies.
questions.explanation: Ideas occur in regular order — that is nature. He is not discarding physics as a pattern of ideas.

questions.prompt: A plausible misreading is that Berkeley

options.text: claims tables vanish when we blink, with no God to sustain the order of ideas

questions.explanation: Divine perception (and the stability of laws) is how he avoids the ‘vanishing furniture’ joke.

recapQuiz.title: Ideas and qualities: recap
recapQuiz.intro: No innatism, primary/secondary, then esse is percipi.

questions.prompt: Locke’s anti-innatism claims that

options.text: apparent innateness is explained by teaching and reason; universal consent is missing

questions.explanation: I.2. Then II fills the paper from sensation and reflection.

questions.prompt: Primary vs secondary qualities distinguish

options.text: bulk/figure/motion as in bodies vs powers to produce color/taste that do not resemble those ideas
innate vs adventitious ideas as Descartes listed them

questions.explanation: II.8. Berkeley will deny the material substratum that was supposed to hold the powers.

questions.prompt: Berkeley’s idealism keeps

options.text: spirits and a God who sustains the order of ideas — not solipsism as the conclusion
abstract general triangles as Locke’s theory needs them
the cogito as the only spirit

questions.explanation: The vanishing-furniture joke ignores God and laws of nature as patterns of ideas.

questions.prompt: Personal identity in Locke II.27 is sameness of soul-substance as such.
questions.explanation: It is sameness of consciousness, a forensic notion. Berkeley’s sitting was not that chapter, but the unit includes it.

questions.prompt: The unit’s arc is that empiricism

options.text: first fills the mind from experience, then comes under pressure about what ‘body’ can mean

questions.explanation: Hume is the next unit. Do not skip Berkeley as a joke.

units.title: Hume’s mitigated skepticism
units.professorNote: Five sittings. Causation and induction first; then miracles; then the self; then design. This is the engine room of later philosophy.

assignments.title: Enquiry II and IV: ideas and induction
assignments.author: David Hume
assignments.pages: Enquiry sec. 2 (origin of ideas) and sec. 4 (sceptical doubts)
assignments.why: All ideas copy impressions (with a famous missing-shade exception). Relations of ideas vs matters of fact. Matters of fact rest on cause and effect; cause and effect are not known a priori; the inference from past to future is not demonstrative. This is the problem of induction. If you only remember the slogan, you have not read Section IV.
lookFor: The copy principle, and why the missing shade matters
Relations of ideas vs matters of fact
Why the future resembling the past is not a demonstration
questions: Is the missing shade a counterexample, or a curiosity he can isolate?
What would a ‘justification’ of induction have to look like, if Hume is right about the options?
assignments.nextHint: Sections V and VII: custom, and the idea of necessary connection.

quiz.title: After Enquiry §2 (and the assigned origin of ideas)
quiz.intro: Copy principle, and a test for meaning.

questions.prompt: Hume’s copy principle says that

options.text: simple ideas are copies of impressions; where an alleged idea has no impression, suspect a confusion

questions.explanation: The missing shade of blue is the famous apparent exception — note it, don’t let it erase the rule.

questions.prompt: The principle is used as

options.text: a meaning-test: demand the impression from which a philosophical term is copied
Berkeley’s esse is percipi restated without change

questions.explanation: The sitting prepares causation: ‘power’ and ‘necessary connexion’ will be run through this test.

questions.prompt: Hume thinks complex ideas can never be assembled from simpler ones.
questions.explanation: The imagination compounds. The discipline is on simple ideas and empty terms.

assignments.title: Enquiry V and VII: custom and necessity
assignments.author: David Hume
assignments.pages: Enquiry sec. 5 (sceptical solution) and sec. 7 (necessary connexion)
assignments.why: Custom or habit is the skeptical solution: we believe, we are not compelled by insight. Necessary connection is not an impression in the objects; it is the mind’s feeling in the transition. This is the sentence Kant said woke him. Read VII until you can say what is missing when you look at one billiard ball.
lookFor: Custom as the guide of life — not a new demonstration
The hunt for the impression of necessity
Two definitions of cause (regularity vs the mind’s determination)
questions: Does Hume deny causation, or deny a certain idea of it?
If necessity is in the mind, why does science still work?
assignments.nextHint: Miracles, then personal identity, then design.

quiz.title: After Enquiry §§4–5, 7
quiz.intro: Custom, not insight into necessity.

questions.prompt: Matters of fact about the unobserved are, for Hume, founded on

options.text: cause and effect — and the inference from observed to unobserved is not itself demonstrative

questions.explanation: §4: relations of ideas vs matters of fact. The future resembling the past is not a demonstration.

questions.prompt: Necessary connexion, as we have it, is

options.text: an impression of a real glue in objects that the mind reads off
the feeling of determination after custom — an impression of reflection, projected onto the world
denied to exist even as a feeling

questions.explanation: §7: we do not perceive power in the objects. Custom is the guide of life (§5).

questions.prompt: Mitigated skepticism here means

options.text: limiting inquiry to what custom and experience can support, without a Pyrrhonian refusal to live

questions.explanation: The sitting: Hume is not Sextus. He walks out of the study.

questions.prompt: Hume thinks we ought to stop making causal inferences.
questions.explanation: We cannot and should not. The point is what they are, not a ban.

assignments.title: Enquiry X: of miracles
assignments.author: David Hume
assignments.why: A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature. The wise man proportions belief to evidence. Testimony for a miracle must outweigh the uniform experience that constitutes the law — and in practice it never does, given the passions of religion and the love of wonder. This is a rule of historical method, not a proof that God cannot act.
lookFor: The definition of miracle via laws of nature
Why testimony is structurally weaker here than in ordinary history
The practical maxim, as opposed to a metaphysical ban
questions: Does the argument beg the question by assuming the laws cannot be violated?
What would Hume say about a miracle you yourself seemed to see?
assignments.nextHint: The self as a bundle: Treatise I.4.6.

quiz.title: After Enquiry §10
quiz.intro: Testimony vs uniform experience.

questions.prompt: A miracle, in Hume’s definition here, is

options.text: a violation of the laws of nature (as established by uniform experience)

questions.explanation: Without that definition the argument does not start. Do not substitute a looser sense.

questions.prompt: The evidential claim is that

options.text: miracles never happen, as a metaphysical proof
no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle unless the falsehood of the testimony would be more miraculous than the fact — and in practice it is not
experience never supports laws of nature

questions.explanation: It is a rule of evidence, not a laboratory disproof of every report.

questions.prompt: Section 10 argues from the copy principle alone, without weighing kinds of testimony.
questions.explanation: The essay is about testimony, passion, and contrary miracles — not only §2.

assignments.title: Treatise I.4.6: personal identity
assignments.author: David Hume
assignments.why: There is no impression of a simple, continuing self. The mind is a bundle of perceptions in flux, tied by memory and association. Identity is a fiction we substitute, as with a republic or a river. Locke’s forensic person is in trouble — or at least his supporting soul-substance is. This sitting is short and dense. Reread the bundle image until it is not a meme.
lookFor: The failed search for a constant impression of self
The bundle (or theatre) image — and its limits
Memory’s role in the fiction of identity
questions: If there is no self, who is worried about personal identity?
Does Hume explain the feeling of identity, or explain it away?
assignments.nextHint: Dialogues: design, evil, and the limits of natural religion.

quiz.title: After Treatise I.4.6
quiz.intro: The self as a bundle, and a fiction of identity.

questions.prompt: When Hume looks for a self, he finds

options.text: a simple immaterial substance always present
particular perceptions — and no impression of a simple continuing self distinct from them
the cogito as Descartes left it
Locke’s forensic person as a substance

questions.explanation: The bundle is a report of introspection plus an account of why we feign identity.

questions.prompt: We ascribe identity to the mind because

options.text: imagination associates resembling, related perceptions and mistakes succession for one object

questions.explanation: LookFor: the fiction, not a joke about ‘no one is home.’ Agency and morals wait on later books; this sitting is I.4.6.

questions.prompt: Hume claims that personal identity is a demonstrated metaphysical truth like a triangle’s.
questions.explanation: It is a natural belief explained, not a relation of ideas.

assignments.title: Dialogues II, X–XI: design and evil
assignments.author: David Hume
assignments.why: Cleanthes’ design argument from the world’s machine-like order; Philo’s analogical doubts (why this designer, why not a team, a juvenile god, a vegetable). Then evil: the world’s misery as evidence against a morally perfect author, or at least against our analogical theology. You are watching natural religion come apart without a cheap atheist’s victory lap. Note who speaks last, and do not over-identify Hume with one voice.
lookFor: The analogical structure of the design argument
Philo’s competing analogies
The problem of evil as a constraint on what we may infer about the cause of the world
questions: Does Philo refute design, or only our right to a particular picture of the designer?
After Parts X–XI, what if anything remains of ‘natural religion’?
assignments.nextHint: Political and moral Enlightenment: Rousseau, Smith, then Kant’s answer to Hume.

quiz.title: After the Dialogues (assigned parts)
quiz.intro: Design, analogy, and what we may infer.

questions.prompt: The design argument, as Cleanthes urges, infers a designer from

options.text: order and adjustment in nature as like a machine, hence a mind like a human artisan, proportioned to the effect

questions.explanation: Analogy is the engine. Philo will press the disanalogy.

questions.prompt: Philo’s pressure includes that

options.text: there is no order in nature at all
the analogy underdetermines: many causes could produce order; the inference to a unique, infinite, moral author outruns the data

questions.explanation: The sitting: what the assigned parts allow you to conclude — not a biography of Hume.

questions.prompt: A student who thinks the Dialogues simply ‘prove atheism’ has

options.text: quoted Philo’s whole last word without remainder
missed the dramatic underdetermination and the lingering natural belief in order — the text is not a tract

questions.explanation: LookFor was the argument’s limits, not a label.

recapQuiz.title: Hume: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Ideas, causation, miracles, self, and design — one empiricism, five sittings.

questions.prompt: The copy principle is used to

options.text: test whether a philosophical term has an impression — preparing the treatment of power and self

questions.explanation: §2 is not a side essay. Causation and the self inherit the test.

questions.prompt: Causal inference, for Hume, is

options.text: custom after constant conjunction, with necessary connexion as a feeling of determination
insight into a glue in objects

questions.explanation: Mitigated skepticism: we live by it; we do not see into the essence of power.

questions.prompt: Miracles as a topic of evidence depend on

options.text: defining a miracle as any surprise
weighing testimony against uniform experience of laws of nature

questions.explanation: §10 is not §7. Keep the sittings.

questions.prompt: The Treatise on personal identity and the Dialogues on design both show

options.text: the imagination’s (or analogical reason’s) overreach beyond impressions

questions.explanation: Bundle and fiction; underdetermined designer. Different objects, same discipline.

questions.prompt: Hume’s mitigated skepticism is Pyrrhonian refusal to live by appearances.
questions.explanation: He walks out of the study. Sextus was a different unit.

questions.prompt: Kant will inherit from this unit especially

options.text: the interruption of dogmatic necessity — causation as a problem for metaphysics

questions.explanation: The Copernican preface names that interruption.

eras.title: Enlightenment politics and the Copernican turn
eras.intro: Rousseau relocates legitimacy in the general will; Smith explains moral judgment through the impartial spectator; Kant answers Hume by turning the question around: objects conform to our forms of intuition and categories, and morality is autonomy under a universal law. You do not need the whole Critique. You need the turn, and the Groundwork’s formulas.

units.title: Freedom, the general will, sympathy
units.professorNote: Rousseau’s diagnosis and his contract, then Smith’s moral psychology — a different Enlightenment than Kant’s.

assignments.title: Discourse on Inequality, Part I
assignments.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
assignments.work: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
assignments.why: Natural man is not Hobbes’s combatant. Pity, limited needs, and the absence of amour-propre come first; inequality as we know it is a social product. This is a conjectural history in the service of a moral claim: we have made ourselves miserable by institutions we take as nature. The Social Contract will try to name a legitimate bond.
lookFor: Natural vs social inequality
Amour de soi versus amour-propre (as the Discourse sets them up)
Why ‘state of nature’ here is not a lost paradise you could return to by camping
questions: Is this anthropology, or a mirror held up to Paris?
What in Hobbes is being refused at the root?
assignments.nextHint: Social Contract I: the problem of legitimate authority.

quiz.title: After the Discourse on Inequality (assigned part)
quiz.intro: Natural independence, and what society adds.

questions.prompt: Natural man, in this discourse’s conjecture, is marked by

options.text: Hobbesian war as the original fact
limited needs, pity, and independence — inequality as we know it is largely social and historical

questions.explanation: The sitting: a genealogy of inequality, not a field report. Distinguish natural from moral/political inequality.

questions.prompt: Amour-propre (in the story of socialization) differs from amour de soi in that

options.text: it is comparative self-love that needs others’ eyes — a social passion, not mere self-preservation

questions.explanation: A common mix-up is to treat all self-love as vice. Rousseau splits the kinds.

questions.prompt: Rousseau claims the historical state of nature is a documented ethnography of one tribe.
questions.explanation: He says we must conjecture. The method is hypothetical history.

assignments.title: Social Contract I: born free
assignments.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
assignments.why: Man is born free, and everywhere in chains. The problem: find a form of association that defends each with the force of all, while each obeys only himself. The solution named: the social compact, alienation of rights to the whole, the general will. Force is not right. Slavery cannot be made legitimate by conquest. This is the Enlightenment’s most explosive pamphlet-length politics.
lookFor: Why right cannot be reduced to force
The compact’s exchange: natural liberty for civil liberty
The general will as what the compact creates, not a poll of private interests
questions: Can you ‘obey only yourself’ after alienating your rights to the community?
What is the difference between the general will and the will of all?
assignments.nextHint: Book II: law, the legislator, the people.

quiz.title: After Social Contract I
quiz.intro: Freedom, and the strange alienation that saves it.

questions.prompt: Man is born free, and everywhere in chains: the book’s problem is

options.text: how to return to the forests
what could make that subjection legitimate — a form of association that defends each while leaving each as free as before

questions.explanation: I.6: the fundamental problem. Legitimacy, not a travel memoir.

questions.prompt: Total alienation to the whole, on Rousseau’s terms, is supposed to

options.text: create a master distinct from the citizens
produce a moral/collective body whose general will is one’s own in the civil state
restore the right of the strongest as such
be a sales contract for one’s labor only
