questions.explanation: The sitting: why this is not Hobbes’s authorization of a person apart. You may still object that it is.

questions.prompt: Book I treats the right of the strongest as a sufficient title to political authority.
questions.explanation: He rejects force as right. That is the clearing for the compact.

assignments.title: Social Contract II: law and the legislator
assignments.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
assignments.why: Sovereignty is inalienable and indivisible. Law is the register of the general will. The legislator is a paradoxical figure: he founds a people that cannot yet found itself. This is where later readers smell danger (the people forced to be free) and where others hear the only serious alternative to representation-as-private-interest. Read the danger and the hope in the same pages.
lookFor: Inalienability of sovereignty
What a law must look like to be general
The legislator’s problem: wisdom without authority of the ordinary kind
questions: Is ‘forced to be free’ a contradiction, a threat, or a theory of education into citizenship?
Could this work in a large commercial state, on Rousseau’s own terms?
assignments.nextHint: Smith: moral judgment without a general will.

quiz.title: After Social Contract II
quiz.intro: General will, and the lawgiver’s paradox.

questions.prompt: The general will is directed to

options.text: the sum of private appetites (will of all) as such
the common interest — it can be mistaken in deliberation but is not defined as a poll of factions

questions.explanation: II.3: will of all vs general will. A common error is to equate them.

questions.prompt: Sovereignty, here, is

options.text: alienable to a representative who then owns it
the exercise of the general will, inalienable and indivisible in the sense Rousseau argues
identical with government as a specialist executive, full stop

questions.explanation: Distinguish sovereignty from government — a lookFor in this sitting.

questions.prompt: The lawgiver is a paradox because

options.text: a people that needs forming is not yet able to will the laws that would form it — so a founder speaks a wisdom the people cannot yet originate
only God legislates in Book II with no remainder

questions.explanation: II.7: take the paradox seriously. It is not a footnote about Lycurgus trivia.

assignments.title: Smith: sympathy and the impartial spectator
assignments.author: Adam Smith
assignments.why: We judge by sympathy: changing places in fancy with the other, and watching whether passions match. The impartial spectator is the internalized other who corrects self-love. This is a moral psychology for commercial society that is not Hobbesian fear and not Rousseau’s general will. Philosophy of economics later split Smith in two; you are reading the moralist first.
lookFor: Sympathy as imaginative exchange, not pity only
Propriety as a mean of passion relative to the spectator
How the impartial spectator is supposed to arise
questions: Can an impartial spectator ever be more than my culture’s average gaze?
What would Kant say is missing if morality is a sentiment of propriety?
assignments.nextHint: Kant: the Copernican turn.

quiz.title: After TMS I.i (and the assigned opening)
quiz.intro: Sympathy, and the impartial spectator in seed.

questions.prompt: Sympathy, for Smith here, is

options.text: a fellow-feeling produced by imagining ourselves in another’s situation — the basis of moral sentiment

questions.explanation: The sitting: moral life begins in spectatorship, not in a lonely law.

questions.prompt: We judge others’ feelings by

options.text: whether we can go along with them — propriety as correspondence of sentiment

questions.explanation: Propriety is the first tool. The impartial spectator develops from this social mirroring.

questions.prompt: Smith’s opening treats self-interest as the only motive, as a certain reading of the Wealth of Nations might suggest.
questions.explanation: TMS begins in sympathy. Do not import a cartoon ‘economic man’ into I.i.

recapQuiz.title: Rousseau and Smith: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Inequality’s genealogy, the compact, and moral spectatorship.

questions.prompt: Rousseau’s natural man, as conjecture, is

options.text: independent, with pity and limited needs — moral inequality is largely historical

questions.explanation: Amour-propre is social. Do not import Hobbes into the forests.

questions.prompt: The Social Contract’s problem is

options.text: how to maximize the right of the strongest
a form of association that is legitimate — freedom through the general will, not force as right
how to restore the Discourse’s forests as policy

questions.explanation: Will of all ≠ general will. Sovereignty ≠ government.

questions.prompt: Smith’s TMS opening locates morals in

options.text: sympathy and propriety — correspondence of sentiment, the seed of an impartial spectator

questions.explanation: Do not read I.i as Wealth of Nations’ ‘economic man.’

questions.prompt: The lawgiver in Contract II is a minor historical footnote with no paradox.
questions.explanation: A people that needs forming cannot yet originate the laws that would form it. That was a sitting.

questions.prompt: This unit prepares Kant by raising

options.text: freedom, law, and a social origin of moral judgment — without yet a categorical imperative

questions.explanation: Kant’s Groundwork will relocate duty. Smith and Rousseau are the social-sentimental and civic-republican foils.

units.title: Kant’s Copernican turn
units.professorNote: Prefaces and Introduction of the first Critique. That is the turn. The Groundwork then does morals without swallowing the whole second Critique.

assignments.title: CPR: Prefaces A and B, Introduction
assignments.author: Immanuel Kant
assignments.selection: Preface to the first edition, Preface to the second, Introduction
assignments.why: Metaphysics has been a battlefield. Hume interrupted dogmatic slumber: if causation is not read off the world, how is necessary science possible? The Copernican hypothesis: objects conform to our way of knowing, not the reverse. Synthetic a priori judgments become the question. The Aesthetic is folded into this sitting via the Introduction’s claim that space and time are the forms of sensibility — if your hosted file’s ‘intro’ stretch includes that turn, stay with it; if not, the Prefaces already name the hypothesis you must be able to state.
lookFor: What the Copernican analogy is supposed to change in the method of metaphysics
Analytic vs synthetic; a priori vs a posteriori — four boxes, one famous problem
Why Hume on causation is the provocation, not a side remark
questions: State the Copernican turn without the word ‘Copernican.’
What is lost if we never get to things in themselves — and what Kant thinks is gained?
assignments.nextHint: Groundwork: the moral law as autonomy.

quiz.title: After the first Critique prefaces (and assigned intro)
quiz.intro: The Copernican turn as a research program.

questions.prompt: Kant’s Copernican analogy proposes that

options.text: the earth is the center of knowledge
objects conform to our way of knowing (space, time, categories), rather than the mind copying things in themselves
Hume is simply mistaken about custom
metaphysics is impossible in every sense

questions.explanation: The sitting: a hypothesis for how a priori knowledge of objects is possible. Not a weather report.

questions.prompt: The Critique limits knowledge to

options.text: appearances (phenomena) — while still making room for faith regarding what cannot be known theoretically

questions.explanation: Bxxx: I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith. Keep the two-object / two-aspect caution as the assigned intro frames it.

questions.prompt: Hume’s role in this preface-story is that

options.text: he interrupted dogmatic metaphysics — the Critique is a response that saves necessity by relocating it

questions.explanation: You were prepared by the Enquiry. Kant names the interruption.

questions.prompt: The Copernican turn means astronomy replaces epistemology.
questions.explanation: It is an analogy about who conforms to whom in cognition.

assignments.title: Groundwork I: good will and duty
assignments.author: Immanuel Kant
assignments.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
assignments.why: Nothing is good without qualification except a good will. The good will is not good by what it effects. Duty is acting from respect for law, not from inclination — even a sympathetic helper may lack moral worth if the maxim is not the law. This offends, and it is supposed to: it isolates the moral motive. Section II will give the formulas.
lookFor: Good will vs gifts of nature and fortune
Acting in accordance with duty vs from duty
The first mention of a universal law as the content of the will
questions: Can a person who enjoys helping still act from duty?
Why isn’t happiness the unqualified good, given Aristotle?
assignments.nextHint: Section II: the categorical imperative in its formulas.

quiz.title: After Groundwork I
quiz.intro: The good will, and duty’s contrast with inclination.

questions.prompt: The good will is good

options.text: only because of what it achieves
without qualification — even if it achieves nothing, unlike talents and gifts of fortune
only in a holy being, never in us

questions.explanation: The opening thesis. Talents can be bad without a good will.

questions.prompt: An action has moral worth, in Section I’s shopkeeper contrast, when

options.text: it accords with duty and is done from immediate inclination only
it is done from duty, not merely in accordance with duty

questions.explanation: LookFor: from duty vs in accordance with duty. The honest shopkeeper is the famous case.

questions.prompt: Kant thinks a person without any inclination toward the good cannot act from duty.
questions.explanation: If anything, the analysis isolates duty more clearly when inclination does not already pull the same way — though the text is subtler than a cartoon of joyless duty.

questions.prompt: The first formulation you meet in this sitting’s trajectory is that of

options.text: acting on a maxim that you can will as universal law (the section’s argument toward the categorical imperative)
the greatest happiness of the greatest number

questions.explanation: Section I arrives at the CI from common moral cognition. Section II will unpack formulas.

assignments.title: Groundwork II: the categorical imperative
assignments.author: Immanuel Kant
assignments.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
assignments.selection: Second Section (formulas of universal law, humanity, kingdom of ends)
assignments.why: Hypothetical imperatives depend on ends you happen to have. The categorical imperative does not. Formulas: act only on maxims you can will as universal law; treat humanity as an end, never merely as a means; a kingdom of ends. Autonomy is the will’s property of being a law to itself. Heteronomy is every other principle (happiness, feeling, divine command as external). This is the moral Copernican turn. Mill will deny that you can ignore consequences this way.
lookFor: Categorical vs hypothetical imperatives
At least two formulas, and whether they are supposed to be equivalent
Autonomy vs heteronomy as the source of spurious principles
questions: Does ‘universal law’ rule out too much (the lying example) or too little?
Is treating humanity as an end a different insight, or the same law in another accent?
assignments.nextHint: After Kant: Hegel’s struggle for recognition; Mill’s liberty and utility; then the century’s explosions.

quiz.title: After Groundwork II (and the assigned stretch of III if included)
quiz.intro: Formulas of the categorical imperative.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical imperative is

options.text: conditional on an end you already will — a means-end rule

questions.explanation: The CI is not hypothetical. That contrast is the grammar of Section II.

questions.prompt: The formula of humanity requires that you

options.text: use persons as mere means whenever convenient
treat humanity in yourself and others always as an end, never merely as a means
obey the sovereign as Hobbes’s authorization

questions.explanation: LookFor: not a slogan. False promising and the ‘mere means’ test were the sitting’s work.

questions.prompt: Autonomy, here, is

options.text: the will’s property of being a law to itself — the third formula’s kingdom of ends gathers legislators

questions.explanation: Heteronomy is when the law comes from an object of desire or an external authority as such.

questions.prompt: Kant thinks the moral law is a piece of advice based on what typically makes people happy.
questions.explanation: That would be a hypothetical imperative of prudence, not a categorical one.

recapQuiz.title: Kant: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Objects conforming to cognition, then a good will and a law the will gives itself.

questions.prompt: The Copernican turn in the first Critique’s prefaces is that

options.text: objects of knowledge conform to our forms of knowing, so a priori knowledge of appearances is possible
things in themselves are known as tables

questions.explanation: Room for faith is the other half of the limit of knowledge.

questions.prompt: Groundwork I’s good will is good

options.text: without qualification, and moral worth attaches to action from duty, not merely in accordance with it

questions.explanation: The shopkeeper is the contrast case.

questions.prompt: Groundwork II’s humanity formula forbids

options.text: treating persons merely as means — as in a lying promise that uses another’s agency
all hypothetical imperatives in technical contexts

questions.explanation: Hypothetical vs categorical is the grammar; autonomy vs heteronomy is the third formula’s point.

questions.prompt: Kant thinks the moral law is advice about what typically produces happiness.
questions.explanation: That is prudence’s hypothetical imperative, not the CI.

questions.prompt: Hume’s custom and Kant’s categories differ in that Kant

options.text: relocates necessity in the subject’s way of knowing (and in practical reason’s law), rather than leaving causation as habit only

questions.explanation: That is why the era ordered Hume then Kant.

eras.title: German idealism and the nineteenth century
eras.intro: Kant’s dualisms do not stay still. Hegel makes recognition a social process; Schopenhauer names will beneath representation; Mill rebuilds morals and liberty without Kantian form; Kierkegaard refuses the System; Marx turns Hegel on history and class; Nietzsche genealogizes morals. Read selections, not systems. The assignment is the move, not the monument.

units.title: Recognition and will
units.professorNote: Hegel’s lordship and bondage is the one stretch of the Phenomenology that a first course must have. Schopenhauer is the no that follows the yes of idealism.

assignments.title: Hegel: lordship and bondage
assignments.author: G. W. F. Hegel
assignments.pages: Phenomenology: Independence and Dependence of Self-Consciousness (Baillie)
assignments.why: Self-consciousness exists only as recognized. Two selves meet; a struggle; one becomes lord, one bondsman. The twist: the lord is stuck in a dead end of consumption, while the bondsman’s work on the thing becomes a path to independent consciousness. This is not a history of slavery as such. It is a claim about how a self becomes a self. Marx and later recognition theory start here. Baillie is 1910 and public domain; later translations are better but not hostable.
lookFor: Why recognition cannot be one-sided
The struggle and the roles of lord and bondsman
Why work, not victory, becomes the engine of a new self-consciousness
questions: Is the bondsman’s ‘independence’ a liberation you would want, or only a stage?
What in Descartes’ cogito is being refused by making the self social from the start?
assignments.nextHint: Schopenhauer: the world as will, not as Hegelian spirit.

quiz.title: After the lordship/bondage sitting
quiz.intro: Self-consciousness that needs another.

questions.prompt: The struggle to the death is about

options.text: recognition: each self-consciousness wants to be acknowledged as not a mere thing

questions.explanation: The sitting: desire and recognition, not a war movie. Life is staked because a life without recognition is not yet self-consciousness.

questions.prompt: The lord’s position is unstable because

options.text: he depends on the bondsman and on a recognition that, coming from a reduced other, cannot satisfy
Hegel prefers slavery as a final truth

questions.explanation: The twist: the working consciousness finds itself in the formed thing. Do not stop at ‘master wins.’

questions.prompt: Independent self-consciousness, on this account, is achieved by ignoring others.
questions.explanation: It is essentially social. That is the break with a lonely cogito as the whole story.

assignments.title: Schopenhauer: world as idea and as will
assignments.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
assignments.work: The World as Will and Idea
assignments.translator: R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp
assignments.selection: Opening of Book I (world as idea) and Book II (world as will)
assignments.pages: World as Will and Idea, openings of Books I–II
assignments.why: The world is my idea: Kant’s objects-as-appearances, said without Kant’s remaining optimism about practical reason. Beneath representation, will — blind striving, objectified in bodies and in nature. Nietzsche will twist this. For now, feel the metaphysical pessimism as a philosophical thesis, not a mood.
lookFor: ‘The world is my idea’ — what is being claimed about subject and object
Will as the thing-in-itself, in Schopenhauer’s appropriation of Kant
Why this picture leans toward suffering rather than progress
questions: Has he named the thing-in-itself, against Kant’s ban, or only relabeled it?
What ethics would follow if will is endless striving?
assignments.nextHint: Mill: a different nineteenth century — utility and the liberty of the individual.

quiz.title: After The World as Will (assigned books)
quiz.intro: Representation, and will as the inner of phenomena.

questions.prompt: The world as representation is

options.text: object for a subject — Kant’s phenomena radicalized; the thing in itself is named will

questions.explanation: Book I: the world is my representation. Book II: will as the kernel.

questions.prompt: Will, in the assigned stretch, is

options.text: a rational planner like Kant’s good will
blind striving that objectifies in nature and in us — intellect is its instrument, not its master

questions.explanation: LookFor: not moral will. Metaphysical will. Art and denial of the will are later therapy, if your sitting reached them.

questions.prompt: Schopenhauer thinks sufficient reason explains the will as it does objects in representation.
questions.explanation: The will as thing in itself is precisely not an object in the principle of sufficient reason’s net — that is the Kantian inheritance twisted.

units.title: Mill: utility and liberty
units.professorNote: Utilitarianism first, so On Liberty is not a free-speech slogan detached from a theory of the good.

assignments.title: Utilitarianism I–II
assignments.author: John Stuart Mill
assignments.selection: Chapters I–II (hosted file emphasizes II; read I in any complete edition if II assumes it)
assignments.why: The right act promotes happiness. Mill’s defense against ‘swine’ is qualitative: some pleasures are higher, as competent judges attest. This is both a reply to Kant (consequences matter) and a reply to crude Bentham. Watch the competent-judge move: it is empirical in ambition and aristocratic in method.
lookFor: The greatest happiness principle, stated without cartoon
Higher and lower pleasures — the test of competent judges
How this is supposed to avoid reducing humans to swine
questions: Do competent judges smuggle in a non-utilitarian ranking of lives?
Can you will a lying maxim as universal law and still be a utilitarian? Where do the theories split?
assignments.nextHint: On Liberty: the harm principle and individuality.

quiz.title: After Utilitarianism ch. 2
quiz.intro: Quality of pleasure, and the competent judges.

questions.prompt: Mill’s utilitarianism takes as the standard

options.text: happiness as pleasure and absence of pain — of all concerned, with a distinction of higher and lower pleasures

questions.explanation: Ch. 2: not a cartoon of swine. Quality is the point of the sitting.

questions.prompt: Higher pleasures are identified by

options.text: the preference of competent judges who have experienced both kinds

questions.explanation: A common misreading is that Mill simply asserts poetry is nicer. The test is comparative verdict of the competent.

questions.prompt: Mill claims a dissatisfied Socrates is not more worthy than a satisfied fool, because quantity of pleasure is all.
questions.explanation: The famous line goes the other way: better Socrates dissatisfied. That is quality.

questions.prompt: ‘Greatest happiness’ as Mill states it is not

options.text: impartial among persons in the theory’s intent
a license for the agent to count only a private clique’s pleasures as the whole of the standard
a contrast with Kantian duty as motive

questions.explanation: The standard is the general happiness. Motive may still be local; that is a distinction Mill himself draws.

assignments.title: On Liberty I–II: the harm principle
assignments.author: John Stuart Mill
assignments.why: The sole end for which power may be exercised over a member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. Chapter II: liberty of thought and discussion — not because all opinions are true, but because truth needs collision, and because silencing assumes infallibility. This is the classic liberal sitting. Read the exceptions (children, ‘backward’ societies) as part of the argument, not as an awkward footnote you skip.
lookFor: The harm principle, including what it is not (not: offense, not: paternalism for adults)
The infallibility argument against silencing
Dead dogma vs living truth
questions: Is ‘harm’ stable enough to limit the state, or does it expand on demand?
Does the discussion of ‘barbarians’ undermine the universality of the principle?
assignments.nextHint: Chapter III: individuality as an element of well-being.

quiz.title: After On Liberty I–II
quiz.intro: The harm principle, and free discussion.

questions.prompt: The harm principle says that

options.text: the state may coerce to make you virtuous for your own good as such
the only purpose for which power may be rightfully exercised over a member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others

questions.explanation: Ch. 1: not a small slogan. Paternalism is the target.

questions.prompt: Mill defends freedom of discussion because

options.text: silencing an opinion robs the human race — if right, of truth; if wrong, of a clearer collision with error

questions.explanation: Ch. 2: three cases (true, false, mixed). LookFor was the argument, not ‘be nice.’

questions.prompt: On Liberty I treats self-regarding faults as properly punished by the magistrate as crimes.
questions.explanation: The split self-regarding / other-regarding is the point of the principle — with all the difficulties you were asked to feel.

assignments.title: On Liberty III: individuality
assignments.author: John Stuart Mill
assignments.why: Individuality is not a taste for eccentricity. It is a condition of human development and of social progress. Custom is a despot; genius needs oxygen. This chapter connects the harm principle to Mill’s idea of a flourishing human — and shows why liberty is, for him, a utilitarian instrument, not a side-constraint from nowhere.
lookFor: Why individuality is an ingredient of well-being, not a luxury
The despotism of custom
How this chapter is supposed to support, not compete with, utility
questions: Can a utilitarian really protect the eccentric when the majority’s happiness would crush them?
What would Rousseau’s general will say to this praise of being unlike others?
assignments.nextHint: Kierkegaard against the System; Marx against the class structure of that same century.

quiz.title: After On Liberty III
quiz.intro: Individuality as a good, not a mood.

questions.prompt: Individuality matters, for Mill, because

options.text: eccentricity is always morally better than virtue
human capacities develop by choice and experiments in living — a social good, not only a private taste

questions.explanation: Ch. 3: genius and originality as conditions of progress. Not a teenage manifesto.

questions.prompt: The despotism of custom is dangerous because

options.text: it freezes a type and prevents the competition of ways of life that progress requires

questions.explanation: The sitting: why liberty is not only non-interference with trade.

questions.prompt: Mill thinks a person should never consider others’ well-being when choosing a way of life.
questions.explanation: The harm principle still binds. Individuality is not a right to injure.

recapQuiz.title: Mill: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Higher pleasures, harm, and individuality as a social good.

questions.prompt: Utilitarianism ch. 2’s distinctive claim is that

options.text: pleasures differ in kind, as competent judges who know both would prefer
Kant’s good will is the standard

questions.explanation: Socrates dissatisfied vs fool satisfied is the slogan of quality.

questions.prompt: The harm principle limits coercion to

options.text: making you virtuous for your own good as such
preventing harm to others — against paternalism as a title

questions.explanation: On Liberty I. Chapter II then defends discussion as a social good.

questions.prompt: Individuality in ch. III is

options.text: experiments in living as a condition of human development and progress
the despotism of custom under a new name

questions.explanation: Eccentricity is not automatically virtue; custom’s freeze is the danger.

questions.prompt: Mill thinks silencing a false opinion costs the human race nothing.
questions.explanation: Even a false opinion, colliding with truth, clarifies. That was ch. II.

questions.prompt: Relative to Kant, Mill’s standard of right is

options.text: the general happiness (with quality), not a formal law of maxims as the first word

questions.explanation: The unit is a rival modern moral philosophy, not a footnote to the Groundwork.

units.title: Existence and historical materialism
units.professorNote: Two refusals of Hegelian reconciliation: the single individual before God, and class struggle as the motor of history.

assignments.title: Kierkegaard: Fear and Trembling (Hollander)
assignments.author: Søren Kierkegaard
assignments.selection: The Fear and Trembling section in Hollander’s 1923 Selections
assignments.why: Abraham’s trial cannot be mediated into the ethical universal. Faith is a paradox: the single individual is higher than the universal, in fear and trembling. Hollander’s 1923 translation is public domain and incomplete as a scholarly edition; it is enough to meet the knight of faith against Hegelian ‘both/and.’ If you later read a complete Hong or Hannay, you are deepening, not replacing, this sitting.
lookFor: Why Abraham cannot explain himself in ethical language
The teleological suspension of the ethical — what is suspended, and toward what
How this is a refusal of Hegel’s mediation
questions: Is the knight of faith distinguishable from a murderer except by an inner we cannot see?
What remains of Kantian universal law if this paradox is allowed?
assignments.nextHint: Marx: history as class struggle, not as the odyssey of Spirit.

quiz.title: After Fear and Trembling (assigned)
quiz.intro: Abraham, and a suspension that is not ethics as usual.

questions.prompt: The teleological suspension of the ethical names

options.text: a permission to murder for convenience
Abraham’s relation to Isaac as not justifiable in universal ethical terms — a private absolute duty to God

questions.explanation: The sitting: the knight of faith vs the tragic hero who remains in the ethical.

questions.prompt: Why Abraham cannot speak, on this reading, is that

options.text: the ordeal cannot be translated into the universal without ceasing to be faith — language is the ethical’s medium
Johannes de Silentio is a historian

questions.explanation: Silence is a philosophical claim about the incommensurable, not a plot device only.

questions.prompt: Fear and Trembling presents Abraham as a Hegelian ethical exemplar of family life.
questions.explanation: The whole point is the collision with the ethical universal.

assignments.title: Manifesto, parts I–II
assignments.author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
assignments.why: The history of hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. The bourgeoisie has played a revolutionary part — and produced its own gravediggers. Part II: the relation of communists to the proletariat; abolition of bourgeois property as the key. Read it as a philosophical claim about what drives history and what a person is (a social ensemble), not only as a political pamphlet you already have opinions about.
lookFor: Class struggle as the structure of history
The bourgeoisie’s revolutionary and self-undermining role
What ‘abolition of private property’ targets (bourgeois property, not every toothbrush)
questions: Is this a moral condemnation, a scientific prediction, or both?
How does the bondsman’s labor in Hegel become, here, a world-historical class?
assignments.nextHint: Nietzsche: morals have a history that is not Mill’s progress or Marx’s class — a genealogy of values.

quiz.title: After Manifesto I–II
quiz.intro: History as class struggle, and a program.

questions.prompt: The history of hitherto existing society is, in the Manifesto’s opening claim,
questions.explanation: Bourgeois and proletarian is the modern simplification of that history.

questions.prompt: The bourgeoisie is revolutionary, on this account, because

options.text: it constantly revolutionizes production and draws the whole world into its mode — and so produces its own grave-diggers

questions.explanation: LookFor: the double movement. Praise of bourgeois dynamism is not a slip.

questions.prompt: Section II’s communism is presented as

options.text: a return to primitive scarcity as an ideal
an abolition of bourgeois property as class property — not of all personal appropriation as such, in the pamphlet’s rhetoric
identical with Kant’s kingdom of ends
a defense of the absolute monarch

questions.explanation: Read the charges and replies. Do not substitute a later textbook for the pamphlet’s sentences.

questions.prompt: The Manifesto treats the state as a neutral referee above classes.
questions.explanation: Political power is organized power of one class for oppressing another — in this text’s terms.

units.title: Nietzsche’s genealogy
units.professorNote: Genealogy first (the method), then a few Gay Science blows (God, recurrence) so you have the temperature as well as the argument.

assignments.title: Genealogy, First Essay: good and evil
assignments.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
assignments.selection: Preface (if in your stretch) and First Essay
assignments.why: ‘Good’ did not always mean the opposite of evil. Knightly-aristocratic values (good/bad) are inverted by a priestly slave revolt into good/evil — a moralization of ressentiment. This is a historical hypothesis with philosophical teeth: our highest values may be an inverted wound. You need not accept the history to feel the method: ask who needed this value, and what it did.
lookFor: Good/bad vs good/evil as two value-systems
Ressentiment as a creative, not merely reactive, force
What a ‘slave revolt in morals’ is supposed to have changed
questions: If this genealogy is true, does it refute the values, or only explain them?
Where would Mill’s competent judges sit in this story?
assignments.nextHint: Second Essay: guilt, debt, bad conscience.

quiz.title: After Genealogy I
quiz.intro: Good/bad, and the slave revolt in morals.

questions.prompt: Noble good/bad, in Essay I, contrasts with

options.text: good/evil as the resentful inversion that makes the strong ‘evil’ and the weak ‘good’

questions.explanation: LookFor: two pairs of terms. Mixing them is the usual mistake.

questions.prompt: Ressentiment is creative in the slave revolt because

options.text: it produces a new valuation — a spiritual revenge — rather than a mere complaint
it is identical with pity as Smith describes it

questions.explanation: The sitting: morality has a history and a psychology. Not a refutation by insult.

questions.prompt: Nietzsche’s first essay is mainly a biography of Jesus as a historical individual.
questions.explanation: It is a typology of valuation (with a notorious closing on the ‘Redeemer’). Stay with the good/evil mechanism.

assignments.title: Genealogy, Second Essay: guilt and bad conscience
assignments.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
assignments.why: Guilt as Schuld: debt. Memory is burned in by pain. Bad conscience is the instinct of cruelty turned inward when it cannot discharge outward. The sovereign individual, the right to make promises — a late product, not the starting point of morality. This essay is the darker half of the method. It will haunt Freud and every later story about internalization.
lookFor: The creditor–debtor origin of guilt
Bad conscience as internalized cruelty
The ‘sovereign individual’ as an achievement, not a given
questions: Does this reduce justice to cruelty with a ledger, or explain how justice became possible?
What would Augustine’s divided will look like in this vocabulary?
assignments.nextHint: Gay Science: the madman, and the heaviest weight.

quiz.title: After Genealogy II
quiz.intro: Conscience, debt, and the badly remembered animal.

questions.prompt: The promise-making animal requires

options.text: forgetting as a force, and a memory of the will — a history of pain as mnemonics
a social contract in Hobbes’s exact sense

questions.explanation: LookFor: memory, pain, and the right to make promises. Bad conscience is a later internalization.

questions.prompt: Bad conscience arises, on this story, when

options.text: instincts that cannot discharge outwardly turn inward — the soul’s interior as a result, not a given

questions.explanation: Internalization is the genealogical claim. Guilt as debt is the linguistic-legal thread.

questions.prompt: Essay II treats guilt as a timeless fact of reason with no history.
questions.explanation: The whole essay is the history. That is the method you were assigned.

assignments.title: Gay Science: the madman and recurrence
assignments.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
assignments.selection: The hosted selection, with attention to the madman (§125) and the heaviest weight (§341) in Common’s numbering
assignments.why: The madman: God is dead, and we have killed him — not a cheer, a diagnosis of a vacuum. Eternal recurrence as the heaviest weight: would you will this life again, innumerable times? These are tests of affirmation after genealogy has unhooked you from inherited tables. Common’s English is of its time; the thoughts are the assignment.
lookFor: Why ‘God is dead’ is a claim about us, not a cosmic autopsy
Recurrence as an ethical test rather than an astrophysical theory
How this follows the Genealogy rather than replacing it
questions: Is the madman announcing liberation, mourning, or both?
What would it mean to fail the recurrence test and still go on living as before?
assignments.nextHint: America and Cambridge: pragmatism and the analytic turn, still in the public domain.

quiz.title: After the Gay Science (assigned)
quiz.intro: The death of God as an event in meaning.

questions.prompt: ‘God is dead’ in the assigned stretch is primarily

options.text: a claim that the Christian-Platonic horizon of meaning has collapsed — with consequences we have not yet absorbed
a proof that no one ever believed

questions.explanation: The madman is about the event’s unreadiness, not a joke at priests only.

questions.prompt: A philosophical task this sitting names is

options.text: returning to Burnet’s Milesians as sufficient
what values and sciences still presuppose the dead God — and what cheerfulness or weight that implies

questions.explanation: LookFor was the diagnosis, not a Wikipedia timeline of Nietzsche’s life.

questions.prompt: The Gay Science sitting is mainly a system of metaphysics like the Monadology.
questions.explanation: It is aphoristic diagnosis. The quiz checks the event, not a table of categories.

recapQuiz.title: Nietzsche: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Two pairs of values, the animal that promises, and a dead God.

questions.prompt: Genealogy I’s slave revolt turns

options.text: good/bad into the same as good/evil
noble good/bad into a resentful good/evil that brands the strong as evil

questions.explanation: Keep the two pairs. Mixing them is the unit’s favorite error.

questions.prompt: Genealogy II’s bad conscience is

options.text: instincts turned inward — interiority as a historical product, with guilt as a debt-story

questions.explanation: The promise-making animal needed a memory made of pain first.

questions.prompt: ‘God is dead’ in the Gay Science sitting is

options.text: the collapse of a horizon of meaning whose consequences are not yet absorbed

questions.explanation: The madman is about unreadiness, not a joke only.

questions.prompt: Ressentiment, in Essay I, is merely a complaint with no new values.
questions.explanation: It is creative: a new table of values. That was the lookFor.

questions.prompt: This unit follows Marx and Kierkegaard in the era because

options.text: history, faith’s collision with the ethical, and class struggle are already on the table — revaluation is another historical psychology

questions.explanation: The nineteenth century is several hammers, not one doctrine.

eras.title: The turn into the twentieth century
eras.intro: Two families, still public domain: American pragmatism (ideas as habits of action; race and double consciousness as philosophy) and the early analytic sequence (Moore’s open question, Russell’s problems, the Tractatus’s picture theory and silence). After 1922 the legal situation changes. This era is the last stretch you can read entire in the app.

units.title: Pragmatism and double consciousness
units.professorNote: Peirce’s maxim, James’s application, Dewey’s reconstruction, Du Bois’s veil. This is not a detour from ‘real’ philosophy.

assignments.title: Peirce: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
assignments.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
assignments.work: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
assignments.why: The meaning of a conception is the sum of its practical bearings — conceivable effects on conduct and experience. Belief is a habit of action. This is the pragmatic maxim, before James popularizes and (Peirce thinks) loosens it. Read it as a third way between Cartesian intuition and British psychology.
lookFor: The four methods of fixing belief (briefly) and why science is preferred
The pragmatic maxim, in Peirce’s wording
What would make two ideas the same idea
questions: Does this reduce truth to usefulness, or only clarify meaning?
How would Descartes’ ‘clear and distinct’ fail this test?
assignments.nextHint: James: pragmatism as a method and as a theory of truth’s cash-value.

quiz.title: After ‘How to Make Our Ideas Clear’
quiz.intro: Belief as a habit, and the pragmatic maxim.

questions.prompt: For Peirce here, belief is

options.text: a private feeling with no effects
a habit of action — doubt is the irritation that inquiry tries to settle

questions.explanation: The paper’s psychology of inquiry is the setup for the maxim.

questions.prompt: The pragmatic maxim says that the meaning of a conception lies in

options.text: the practical effects we conceive the object of the conception to have

questions.explanation: LookFor: effects, not ‘cash value’ as a later slogan only. Hardness as a conception of would-be interactions is the famous example.

questions.prompt: Peirce thinks a perfectly clear idea can still be empty of conceivable practical bearings.
questions.explanation: Clarity in the third grade is those bearings. That is the paper’s point against Cartesian ‘clarity.’

assignments.title: James: Pragmatism, Lectures I–II
assignments.author: William James
assignments.why: The tender-minded and tough-minded; pragmatism as a mediator. Lecture II: the pragmatic method, and Peirce named. Truth as what works in the way of belief — James’s more expansive cash-value talk. Keep Peirce in the room so you can see where James widens the maxim toward temperament and religion.
lookFor: The two temperaments and why philosophy has been their war
The pragmatic method as a way of settling metaphysical disputes
Where James’s ‘what works’ might outrun Peirce’s conceivable effects
questions: Is pragmatism a theory of meaning, of truth, or of how to live among options?
What dispute (free will, the Absolute) is supposed to dissolve when you ask for cash-value?
assignments.nextHint: The Will to Believe: when evidence is not enough and the option is forced.

quiz.title: After Pragmatism (assigned lectures)
quiz.intro: Truth in the making, without ‘whatever I wish.’

questions.prompt: James’s pragmatism treats a true idea as

options.text: a copy of a static reality with no further office
one that we can assimilate, validate, corroborate, and verify — truth happens to an idea
whatever is expedient in the way of our private cheating

questions.explanation: LookFor: the cash-value lecture’s care. ‘Expedient’ is fenced by the long run and the face of other truths.

questions.prompt: A common misreading to refuse is that James

options.text: means that a comforting falsehood is true if it pleases me this afternoon
inherits Peirce’s maxim with a difference

questions.explanation: The sitting asked you to state the view so it is not a joke. Other truths and the long run are the fence.

questions.prompt: James presents pragmatism as a method of settling metaphysical disputes by tracing practical differences.
questions.explanation: That is the method lecture. If two formulas make no difference in practice, the dispute is idle.

assignments.title: James: The Will to Believe
assignments.author: William James
assignments.why: When an option is living, forced, and momentous, and intellect cannot decide, it can be rational to let the passional nature choose — especially in religion and trust. Clifford’s ‘insufficient evidence’ is refused as a moral rule for all belief. This is not a license for wishful thinking about ordinary facts. Watch the restrictions.
lookFor: Living / forced / momentous options
The quarrel with Clifford
Why friendship and religion are the examples, not chemistry
questions: Does James license believing what is false if it pays?
How does this sit with Peirce’s method of science?
assignments.nextHint: Dewey: philosophy reconstructed as a social instrument.

quiz.title: After ‘The Will to Believe’
quiz.intro: Forced, live, momentous options.

questions.prompt: James’s thesis is that

options.text: we should always wait for sufficient evidence in every domain, including the religious
when an option is living, forced, and momentous, and intellect cannot decide, it can be lawful to will a belief that runs ahead of proof

questions.explanation: The three marks of the genuine option are the lookFor. Without them the essay is misread as ‘believe whatever.’

questions.prompt: Clifford’s ethic (‘it is wrong always to believe on insufficient evidence’) is rejected when

options.text: waiting itself is a kind of bet — as in friendship or religion — so ‘neutrality’ is already a choice

questions.explanation: The sitting: not a license for wishful meteorology. The domain is restricted.

questions.prompt: James argues that one ought to will beliefs about next week’s weather without data.
questions.explanation: Weather is not a genuine option of the religious/moral type the essay isolates.

assignments.title: Dewey: Reconstruction in Philosophy I–II
assignments.author: John Dewey
assignments.why: Philosophy is not a rival physics of the eternal. It grows from social crisis and imagination; it should be reconstructed as a method of moral and political intelligence. The 1920 date puts it in the public domain. Later Dewey is often still in copyright — this sitting is the legal, and a fair, introduction.
lookFor: The origin of philosophy in a clash of custom and new knowledge
What ‘reconstruction’ asks philosophers to stop doing
Intelligence as experimental and social, not contemplative only
questions: Is this the end of metaphysics, or a relocation of its job?
What would Kant’s a priori look like if Dewey is right about origins?
assignments.nextHint: Du Bois: the veil, double consciousness — philosophy of a social self.

quiz.title: After Reconstruction in Philosophy (assigned)
quiz.intro: Philosophy as a response to problems of life, not a museum.

questions.prompt: Dewey’s reconstruction aims to

options.text: shift philosophy from allegedly ultimate being toward methods of inquiry that deal with present social and scientific problems
return to the Cave’s prisoners as an ideal

questions.explanation: LookFor: the change in philosophy’s office. Not a biography of Chicago.

questions.prompt: A dualism Dewey wants undone is typically

options.text: knowing vs doing, or a spectator theory of knowledge detached from practice

questions.explanation: Reconstruction is a program. The quiz checks the assigned diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Dewey treats inherited philosophical problems as always merely verbal and never historically rooted in life.
questions.explanation: He historicizes them as responses — then asks whether they still serve.

assignments.title: Du Bois: Of Our Spiritual Strivings
assignments.author: W. E. B. Du Bois
assignments.why: The problem of the twentieth century is the color-line. Double consciousness: seeing oneself through a veil, two souls, two thoughts. This is philosophy of mind and political philosophy at once — a social account of self-knowledge Hegel would recognize and James’s student could write. It belongs in a Western philosophy course because the Western self was never only European.
lookFor: The veil as a structure of seeing and being seen
Double consciousness — not ‘low self-esteem,’ a split of perspectives
How emancipation’s aftermath frames the philosophical problem
questions: Is double consciousness only a wound, or also a way of knowing the world the veil hides from others?
How does this complicate Locke’s and Hume’s first-person self?
assignments.nextHint: Moore, Russell, Wittgenstein: the analytic beginning, still PD.

quiz.title: After The Souls of Black Folk (assigned chapters)
quiz.intro: Double-consciousness as a philosophical structure.

questions.prompt: Double-consciousness names

options.text: the sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of a white world — two-ness of American and Negro

questions.explanation: The sitting: a structure of self-knowledge under domination, not a memoir-only reading.

questions.prompt: The Veil in these pages is

options.text: the barrier that splits worlds of meaning and recognition — Du Bois’s image for lived segregation of experience

questions.explanation: LookFor: the image as analysis. The sorrow songs, if assigned, are evidence, not decoration.

questions.prompt: Du Bois presents the problem of the color-line as merely a failure of individual manners, with no historical structure.
questions.explanation: The opening of the book is a world-historical claim about the twentieth century’s problem.

recapQuiz.title: Pragmatism and Du Bois: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Clear ideas, truth that happens, a right to believe, reconstruction, and double-consciousness.

questions.prompt: Peirce’s maxim locates meaning in

options.text: conceivable practical effects of the object of the conception

questions.explanation: Belief as habit of action is the setup. James will shift the accent.

questions.prompt: James’s truth and will-to-believe, fenced correctly, are not

options.text: ‘whatever comforts me this afternoon is true’ or ‘believe anything about the weather’

questions.explanation: The unit’s two James sittings are easy to parody. The fences were the assignments.

questions.prompt: Dewey’s reconstruction asks philosophy to

options.text: restore a museum of ultimate being as the first office
become methods of inquiry for present problems, undoing spectator dualisms of knowing vs doing

questions.explanation: Then Du Bois is not an optional module: double-consciousness is a structure of knowing under the Veil.

questions.prompt: Double-consciousness is

options.text: seeing oneself through a dominant world’s eyes — two-ness as a philosophical problem of self-knowledge

questions.explanation: The Souls sitting belongs in this unit because pragmatism without the color-line is a truncated American story.

questions.prompt: This unit treats Du Bois as a mere illustration of James’s will to believe.
questions.explanation: The Veil is its own analysis. Do not reduce it to a pragmatist example.

units.title: The early analytic sequence
units.professorNote: Moore’s open question, Russell’s table, induction, the value of philosophy, then the Tractatus in two sittings. After that, copyright walls.

assignments.title: Moore: the open-question argument
assignments.author: G. E. Moore
assignments.selection: Chapter I (subject-matter of ethics; naturalistic fallacy)
assignments.why: Good is a simple, unanalyzable quality. Any identification of good with a natural property (pleasure, evolutionary fitness) leaves an open question: but is that good? This is the naturalistic fallacy as Moore names it. Mill’s utility and Aristotle’s function are in the room. Later metaethics will attack Moore; you need the argument in its original force.
lookFor: The distinction between good and things that are good
The open-question argument
What ‘naturalistic fallacy’ does and does not mean (not: ‘never mention nature’)
questions: Does the open question prove simplicity, or only our linguistic habits?
How would Mill answer: is ‘pleasure is good’ tautological on his view?
assignments.nextHint: Russell: appearance, matter, and why philosophy is not just tables.

quiz.title: After Principia Ethica (assigned opening)
quiz.intro: The naturalistic fallacy, and good as simple.

questions.prompt: Moore claims that ‘good’ is

options.text: a simple, unanalyzable non-natural property — defining it as some natural property is the naturalistic fallacy

questions.explanation: LookFor: simple/indefinable, and the fallacy as Moore states it (not later textbook variants only).

questions.prompt: The open-question argument is meant to show that

options.text: for any proposed analysis ‘good = X,’ it remains an open question whether X is good — so the analysis fails

questions.explanation: You may reject the argument. You must state it as a test of definitions.

questions.prompt: Moore thinks ethics should begin by defining good as evolutionary fitness.
questions.explanation: That would be a naturalistic identification of the kind he attacks.

assignments.title: Russell: appearance, acquaintance, description
assignments.author: Bertrand Russell
assignments.pages: Problems of Philosophy chs. I, V (1912)
assignments.why: The table as a lesson: sense-data vs physical object. Then: knowledge by acquaintance and by description — how we can think about things we are not acquainted with. This is the analytic classroom’s first morning. It is also a reply to idealism (Berkeley) without naïve realism.
lookFor: Why the table’s appearance is not simply the table
Sense-data as what we are directly acquainted with
Knowledge by description as the bridge to other minds and to physics
questions: Has Russell refuted Berkeley, or only offered a different hypothesis?
What are you acquainted with, if not the table?
assignments.nextHint: Induction, and why philosophy is still worth doing.

quiz.title: After Problems of Philosophy (appearance)
quiz.intro: The table, sense-data, and what we may still know.

questions.prompt: Russell’s table example is meant to show that

options.text: what is immediately known in seeing is not the public table as physics describes it, but sense-data

questions.explanation: Appearance vs reality is the sitting’s tool. Idealism is a live option he will not simply swallow.

questions.prompt: A sense-datum, here, is

options.text: the color-patch, hardness, etc., immediately present in experience
the thing in itself as Kant’s noumenon

questions.explanation: LookFor: the distinction. Knowledge by acquaintance vs description waits in nearby chapters if assigned.

questions.prompt: Russell uses the table to prove that science is false.
questions.explanation: He is locating what is certain in perception so that physical objects can be inferred — a problem, not a dismissal.

assignments.title: Russell: induction and the value of philosophy
assignments.author: Bertrand Russell
assignments.why: The principle of induction cannot be proved by experience without circularity; we assume it. Chapter XV: the value of philosophy is in the questions, the enlargement of the self, not in a body of settled doctrine. After Hume and before the Tractatus, this is a humane analytic credo. It is also your permission to keep going when systems fail.
lookFor: Why induction is a principle, not a theorem of experience
What philosophy is not (a rival of the special sciences’ results)
The enlargement of the not-Self as a value
questions: Is Russell’s induction principle a confession of Hume’s point or an answer to it?
After this chapter, what would it mean for this course to ‘finish’?
assignments.nextHint: Tractatus: the picture theory, then silence.

quiz.title: After Problems of Philosophy (induction)
quiz.intro: The principle we cannot prove and cannot do without.

questions.prompt: The problem of induction, as Russell states it, is that

options.text: the inference from ‘this has happened’ to ‘it will happen’ is not logically guaranteed, yet science and life require it
Hume already solved it by custom, so there is no problem

questions.explanation: The sitting continues Hume without stopping at therapy. Russell wants the principle named.

questions.prompt: Russell’s attitude is roughly that

options.text: we must accept a principle of induction (or equivalent) as a postulate of knowledge, not a theorem from experience alone
the copy principle proves the future
Kant’s categories are unnecessary to mention

questions.explanation: LookFor: postulate vs proof. A common error is to think he ‘refutes’ Hume by ignoring him.

questions.prompt: This chapter claims induction is a demonstration like arithmetic.
questions.explanation: If it were, it would not be the problem of philosophy it is.

assignments.title: Tractatus 1–5: world, picture, proposition
assignments.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
assignments.why: The world is all that is the case. A proposition is a picture of a state of affairs. Logical form is shown, not said. Ogden’s 1922 translation is public domain. You will later hear that Wittgenstein rejected this book. Read it first as if he meant it. Do not hunt mysticism yet; hunt the picture theory.
lookFor: 1–1.2: world as facts, not things
The picture theory: how a proposition can be true or false
What cannot be said but only shown (logical form)
questions: If the limits of language are the limits of the world, what happens to ethics and the self?
Is this metaphysics, or a ban on metaphysics?
assignments.nextHint: The ending: what we cannot speak about.

quiz.title: After Tractatus (assigned early propositions)
quiz.intro: The world as facts, and the picture.

questions.prompt: ‘The world is all that is the case’ introduces

options.text: a heap of things without structure
the world as the totality of facts, not of things — a logical space of states of affairs

questions.explanation: LookFor: facts vs things. The picture theory is how a proposition can be true or false.

questions.prompt: A proposition is a picture in that

options.text: it is a painting in a gallery
it shares logical form with a possible state of affairs — it shows how things stand if true
it is a private mental image only

questions.explanation: The sitting: sense as possible situation, not as a psychological association.

questions.prompt: The early Tractatus treats ethics and the mystical as additional facts in the world among others.
questions.explanation: That is what the later assigned sitting on the unsayable will press. Early on, the picture is of sayable facts.

assignments.title: Tractatus 6–7: the ladder and silence
assignments.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
assignments.why: The general form of the proposition; then the propositions of the book as elucidatory — a ladder to be thrown away. Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. Ethics, aesthetics, the mystical: they show themselves. This is the last in-app primary text of the course’s PD spine. The next era is a map of what you must obtain legally.
lookFor: The ladder remark — what it does to the status of the book you just read
Proposition 7 as a rule, not a poetic sigh
How this ending both fulfills and undermines the picture theory
questions: If the book is nonsense by its own light, why read it?
What would a second Wittgenstein have to change first: pictures, or silence?
assignments.nextHint: Present-day bridge: in-copyright works, assigned exactly, not hosted.

quiz.title: After Tractatus (assigned later propositions)
quiz.intro: What cannot be said, and the ladder.

questions.prompt: The propositions of the Tractatus, on its own close, are

options.text: elucidations to be thrown away — a ladder — once one has seen the world rightly

questions.explanation: 6.54: throw away the ladder. The sitting is that paradox, not a biography.

questions.prompt: What we cannot speak about

options.text: should be written as more propositions of the same scientific type
we must pass over in silence — ethics, the mystical, the limit of the world are not further facts
does not exist in any sense Wittgenstein cares about
is identical with Hume’s missing shade

questions.explanation: LookFor: the limit of language as the ethical/mystical, not a gag order on poetry only.

questions.prompt: The Tractatus ends by adding extra scientific facts about God as an object in the world.
questions.explanation: God does not reveal himself in the world (6.432). Silence is the point.

recapQuiz.title: Analytic turn: recap
recapQuiz.intro: Good as simple, sense-data, induction, pictures, and silence.

questions.prompt: Moore’s opening move in ethics is that

options.text: good is simple and non-natural; naturalistic identifications fail the open question
the Tractatus already defined good as a fact

questions.explanation: Then Russell relocates philosophy’s first problem in appearance and inference.

questions.prompt: Russell’s table and induction sittings together claim that

options.text: what is immediate is not the public object, and the future is not a theorem — yet we need a principle of induction

questions.explanation: Acquaintance vs the physical; postulate vs proof.

questions.prompt: The Tractatus pair (picture, then silence) says that

options.text: ethics is one more fact in the world
sayable sense is pictorial of facts, and the rest — including the book’s own elucidations — is to be thrown away
ordinary language is the first method of PI already

questions.explanation: The ladder and 7. The Investigations will be a different assignment.

questions.prompt: This unit’s authors all treat ‘good’ as a natural property like yellow.
questions.explanation: Moore’s point is the opposite. The Tractatus then takes ethics off the table of facts.

questions.prompt: The pedagogical hinge into the present-day era is that

options.text: picture-sense and what cannot be said set up both later Wittgenstein and the bibliographic ‘keep going’ sittings

questions.explanation: 1922 is a door, not a wall — but the next door is in copyright.

eras.title: How to keep going
eras.intro: The rest of the century is still in copyright in the United States. You will read it as a student reads assigned chapters: legally, with a physical or licensed copy. The assignments below are exact. They complete the spine: language after the Tractatus, being and existence, the analytic/continental split, justice, power, and inner moral vision. Two final maps tell you how the living debates are clustered so you are not abandoned in 1922.

units.title: Language, being, existence
units.professorNote: Three in-copyright landmarks. The quiz checks whether you found the assigned move, not whether you memorized a biography.

assignments.title: Philosophical Investigations §§1–43
assignments.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
assignments.why: The later Wittgenstein returns to Augustine’s picture of words as names and breaks it: meaning as use, language-games, the impossibility of a private ostensive definition as the whole story. This is the repudiation of the Tractatus’s picture theory from inside the same life. You need a legal copy (Anscombe’s translation is still in copyright).
lookFor: The shopkeeper / five red apples example — what it is for
Language-game as a comparison, not a theory of everything
Why ‘meaning as use’ is not ‘words mean whatever I like’
questions: What in Tractatus 1–4 cannot survive §§1–43?
Is family resemblance a theory of concepts, or a warning against theories of concepts?
assignments.nextHint: Heidegger: the question of being, which the Tractatus treated as something to be silent about — or as nonsense.

source.name: Library or licensed edition
source.edition: Anscombe translation; any standard bilingual edition
source.note: Get a printed or licensed library copy. Do not use a pirated PDF. This course does not host the work.

quiz.title: After Philosophical Investigations §§1–43
quiz.intro: A check on the assigned move, not a biography.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper / five red apples example is meant to show that

options.text: understanding a word is not always having a mental picture of an object — it can be mastery of a technique in a practice
meaning is a private inner pointing that needs no public criteria

questions.explanation: The sitting named this example. It cracks the ‘words as names of objects’ picture without requiring you to quote the book.

questions.prompt: A language-game, as used in these sections, is

options.text: a complete theory of all language
a comparison: looking at primitive practices of using words, to loosen the grip of one picture
a proof that anything I say is correct

questions.explanation: LookFor: comparison, not a theory of everything. ‘Meaning as use’ is not ‘words mean whatever I like.’

questions.prompt: Family resemblance is offered as

options.text: a biological taxonomy of concepts with necessary and sufficient conditions for ‘game’
a warning against assuming one essence hidden behind all uses of a word

questions.explanation: The assignment asked whether it is a theory of concepts or a warning. The latter is the safer reading of §§1–43.

questions.prompt: These sections leave the Tractatus picture theory untouched as an account of ordinary talk.
questions.explanation: Ostension and naming as the whole story is what is under attack — the Tractatus’s picture of sense does not survive unchanged.

assignments.title: Being and Time, Introduction §§1–4
assignments.author: Martin Heidegger
assignments.selection: Introduction, §§1–4 (the question of being; Dasein as the being that asks)
assignments.pages: SZ Introduction §§1–4 (German 1927; English 1962 is in copyright)
assignments.why: The question of being has been forgotten. The being who can ask it is Dasein — existence as ours, not a Cartesian subject with properties. The German original’s US status is not a free pass to host an English translation: Macquarrie (1962) is in copyright, and URAA complications attend the German. Obtain a legal copy. Read only the Introduction’s first four sections; that is the question, not the whole book.
lookFor: Why ‘being’ is not a being among beings
Dasein as the entity that understands being
What is being refused in the Cartesian starting point
questions: Is this a new method, or a new subject-matter?
How would Russell’s table look if the first question were being, not sense-data?
assignments.nextHint: Sartre: existence precedes essence, in public prose.

source.name: Library or licensed edition
source.edition: Macquarrie & Robinson or a later licensed English
source.note: Get a printed or licensed library copy. Do not use a pirated PDF. This course does not host the work. Do not host or download unauthorized scans of the English.

quiz.title: After Being and Time, Introduction §§1–4
quiz.intro: The question of being, not a life of Heidegger.

questions.prompt: ‘Being is not a being’ in this introduction means that

options.text: the question of what it means to be is not answered by pointing to an entity among entities (God, nature, the subject)
Russell’s table is the first question

questions.explanation: LookFor: being is not a being. That is the forgotten question.

questions.prompt: Dasein is introduced as

options.text: a Cartesian ego with properties first
the entity that we are, whose being is an issue for it — the one that understands being
a physical object in space as physics starts
a synonym for ‘human nature’ as a biological essence

questions.explanation: The Cartesian starting point is what is being refused: not a subject inspecting objects as the first move.

questions.prompt: This introduction is best taken as

options.text: the whole of Being and Time
a new subject-matter and method: fundamental ontology via the being that asks

questions.explanation: The assignment: method and subject-matter, not the whole published book.

questions.prompt: Heidegger’s opening treats ‘being’ as one more item in an inventory of beings, like a rare mineral.
questions.explanation: That confusion is exactly the forgetfulness the introduction diagnoses.

assignments.title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
assignments.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
assignments.translator: Carol Macomber or earlier licensed English
assignments.selection: The lecture entire (it is short) with attention to ‘existence precedes essence’ and anguish/abandonment/despair
assignments.why: Existence precedes essence: there is no given human nature that lets you off the hook. In choosing, you choose an image of the human. Anguish, abandonment, despair are technical here, not moods. This is the public, compressed Sartre — a door, not Being and Nothingness. Get a legal edition of the lecture.
lookFor: What ‘existence precedes essence’ denies (a maker’s blueprint for the human)
How a choice is supposed to bind all humans as an image
Why this is offered as a humanism, against the charge of quietism
questions: Does ‘choosing for all’ smuggle in a Kantian universal without the moral law?
What would a materialist (Hobbes, Marx) say is missing from this freedom?
assignments.nextHint: Analytic mid-century: Quine against two dogmas; Anscombe against a certain modern moral philosophy.

source.name: Library or licensed edition
source.edition: Any licensed English of Existentialism Is a Humanism
source.note: Get a printed or licensed library copy. Do not use a pirated PDF. This course does not host the work.

quiz.title: After Existentialism Is a Humanism
quiz.intro: Existence precedes essence — as the lecture defines it.

questions.prompt: ‘Existence precedes essence’ denies that

options.text: there is a maker’s blueprint or given human nature that would tell you in advance what you ought to be

questions.explanation: LookFor: no prefabricated human essence. That is the hook of the lecture.

questions.prompt: In choosing, on Sartre’s public account here, you

options.text: choose only a private whim with no image of the human
choose an image of the human that you take as valid for all — hence anguish
follow a ready-made Kantian table of duties as the whole story

questions.explanation: Anguish, abandonment, despair are technical. Quietism is the charge he answers by calling this a humanism.

questions.prompt: The lecture presents existentialism as an excuse to do nothing, because values are absurd.
questions.explanation: He offers it as a humanism against quietism: one must still choose and invent.

questions.prompt: A serious question the assignment left open is whether ‘choosing for all’

options.text: is a recipe for a banquet
smuggles a universalizing demand without Kant’s moral law as its ground
is identical with Mill’s competent judges

questions.explanation: That was one of the seminar questions. The quiz only needs you to recognize the tension.

assignments.title: Quine: Two Dogmas of Empiricism
assignments.author: W. V. O. Quine
assignments.selection: The whole essay (it is the assignment)
assignments.pages: From a Philosophical Review reprint or From a Logical Point of View — licensed copy
assignments.why: The analytic/synthetic distinction and reductionism are dogmas. Meaning holism: statements meet the tribunal of experience as a corporate body. Empiricism after Hume and Carnap has to live without a sharp language/world split at the sentence level. Do not quote long stretches into notes you share; understand the two dogmas and the holism claim.
lookFor: What the two dogmas are
Why synonymy does not easily save analyticity
The web of belief — what is being said about revision
questions: What happens to Kant’s synthetic a priori if there is no analytic/synthetic cut?
Is holism a skepticism, or a picture of science?

quiz.title: After ‘Two Dogmas of Empiricism’
quiz.intro: The two dogmas, and the web.

questions.prompt: The two dogmas Quine names are

options.text: the analytic/synthetic distinction and reductionism (each statement to a sensory confirming/infirming range)

questions.explanation: LookFor: name the dogmas. Without that, holism has nothing to replace.

questions.prompt: Synonymy does not easily save analyticity, on his argument, because

options.text: explanations of analyticity via synonymy, definition, or necessity tend to circle rather than ground the distinction

questions.explanation: The essay’s first half is this circle. Do not skip it for the slogan ‘web of belief.’

questions.prompt: The web of belief says that

options.text: statements meet the tribunal of experience as a corporate body — any statement can be held true if we make enough adjustments elsewhere

questions.explanation: Holism is a picture of science, not automatically a Pyrrhonian skepticism. That was a seminar question.

questions.prompt: Quine thinks the analytic/synthetic cut is as sharp as Kant needed for the synthetic a priori.
questions.explanation: If the cut goes, that Kantian architecture is among the casualties the assignment asked you to consider.

assignments.title: Anscombe: Modern Moral Philosophy (and a look at Intention §§1–5 if you have it)
assignments.author: G. E. M. Anscombe
assignments.selection: The whole 1958 paper; optionally Intention §§1–5 for the action-theoretic companion
assignments.pages: Philosophy 33 (1958) via library; Intention (1957) is also in copyright
assignments.why: Moral philosophy should be laid aside until we have an adequate philosophy of psychology. The surviving ‘ought’ is a law-sense without a lawgiver — incoherent. This is the paper that helped restart virtue ethics and that refuses both Kantian duty-talk and consequentialism as then practiced. If you also open Intention, take only the opening sections on what it is to act intentionally.
lookFor: Why she wants a philosophy of psychology first
The diagnosis of ‘ought’ as a survivor of a divine-law conception
What she is asking us to stop doing in ethics class
questions: Does this refute Kant, or only a thin classroom Kant?
How would Aristotle’s hexis fit her demand for a psychology?

quiz.intro: Ought without a lawgiver, and a pause.

questions.prompt: Anscombe wants moral philosophy laid aside until we have

options.text: an adequate philosophy of psychology (intention, action, desire) — otherwise ‘ought’ is a surviving fragment
a proof that Aristotle is useless

questions.explanation: LookFor: psychology first. That is the paper’s shock.

questions.prompt: The diagnosis of modern ‘ought’ is that it

options.text: is a survivor of a divine-law conception of ethics, now without a lawgiver — hence incoherent as used

questions.explanation: She is asking a certain ethics class to stop. Both thin duty-talk and a certain consequentialism are in the dock.

options.text: a modern moral philosophy that keeps a law-sense of ‘ought’ while dropping the theological framework that made that sense
Mill’s harm principle as a political rule only

assignments.title: Rawls: Theory of Justice, §§1–4 and 11–14
assignments.author: John Rawls
assignments.selection: Revised edition if possible: ch. 1 §§1–4 (the role of justice; original position) and §§11–14 (two principles, equal liberty, difference principle)
assignments.why: Justice as fairness: the original position and veil of ignorance as a device, not a history. Two principles: equal basic liberties; social and economic inequalities to be arranged for the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, under fair equality of opportunity. This is the social-contract tradition after Hume’s and Rousseau’s and Kant’s — a Kantian procedure with economic content. Library copy. Read the assigned sections only; the book is a doorstop.
lookFor: The original position as a point of view, not a place
The two principles, in order
Why the difference principle is not simple equality and not maximax for the talented
questions: What would Mill’s harm principle say is missing, or already included?
Is the veil of ignorance a moral insight or an economic thought experiment?

quiz.title: After A Theory of Justice (assigned sections)
quiz.intro: A device, two principles, not a history.

questions.prompt: The original position is

options.text: a point of view: parties behind a veil of ignorance choosing principles of justice for the basic structure
a utilitarian sum of pleasures as the first principle

questions.explanation: LookFor: a device, not a place. The veil screens off morally irrelevant bargaining advantages.

questions.prompt: The two principles, in order, concern

options.text: equal basic liberties; then social and economic inequalities arranged for the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, consistent with fair equality of opportunity
the difference principle alone as a complete theory
maximax for the most talented as the first rule

questions.explanation: Priority of liberty, then the difference principle. Not simple equality, not maximax for the gifted.

questions.prompt: The difference principle is not simple equality because

options.text: inequalities can be just if they raise the position of the worst off compared with a more equal scheme

questions.explanation: LookFor: not equality, not maximax for the talented. That is the economic content after Kantian procedure.

questions.prompt: Justice as fairness, in the assigned sections, is presented as a utilitarian average of happiness.
questions.explanation: It is offered as a rival to utilitarianism: the parties would not choose to sacrifice the few as a mere sum.

assignments.title: Foucault: Discipline and Punish, Panopticism
assignments.author: Michel Foucault
assignments.selection: The ‘Panopticism’ chapter (Part III, ch. 3 in the English)
assignments.why: Bentham’s Panopticon becomes a diagram of modern power: visibility, internalization of the gaze, discipline as producing subjects rather than merely forbidding acts. This is a genealogical sitting after Nietzsche, applied to prisons, schools, barracks. Sheridan’s English is in copyright. Obtain it legally. One chapter is enough for the move.
lookFor: The Panopticon as an architectural and social diagram
Power as productive, not only repressive
How this differs from Hobbes’s visible sovereign
questions: Is this a theory of modernity, or a reading of a prison plan overextended?
What would Rawls’s original position look like if the parties were already disciplinary subjects?
assignments.nextHint: Murdoch: moral vision, attention, the Good — against a certain existentialist will.

quiz.title: After the Panopticism chapter
quiz.intro: A diagram of power, not a biography.

questions.prompt: The Panopticon, in this chapter, functions as

options.text: an architectural and social diagram: perpetual possible visibility that produces self-discipline

questions.explanation: LookFor: diagram. Bentham’s plan becomes a figure of modern power.

questions.prompt: Power here is described as

options.text: only the sovereign’s right to kill
productive: it makes subjects, habits, and visibilities, not merely forbidding acts from outside

questions.explanation: The contrast with Hobbes’s visible sovereign was a lookFor. Discipline is capillary, not only spectacular.

questions.prompt: The chapter treats modern punishment as merely the absence of the old scaffold, with no new positive techniques.
questions.explanation: Discipline is a positive technology of bodies and souls — that is the genealogical sting.

questions.prompt: A fair critical question the assignment allowed is whether this is

options.text: a recipe for a panopticon in your house
a reading of a prison plan that may be overextended into a total theory of modernity
identical with Nietzsche’s Genealogy word for word

questions.explanation: Seminar question: theory of modernity vs overextended prison plan. Recognize the stakes.

assignments.title: Murdoch: The Sovereignty of Good (title essay)
assignments.author: Iris Murdoch
assignments.selection: The essay ‘The Sovereignty of Good Over Other Concepts’ (the volume’s central piece)
assignments.pages: The Sovereignty of Good, title essay
assignments.why: Against a picture of the moral agent as a naked will issuing choices: moral life is a matter of vision, attention, unselfing — Platonic Good without cheap mysticism. This is a late-century reply to Sartre and to a certain analytic thinness, written in English you must obtain legally. One essay, read slowly, is the assignment.
lookFor: What is wrong, for her, with existentialist/Kantian will as the whole of morals
Attention (and M’s example of the mother-in-law) as moral activity
The Good as a magnetic, not a chosen, orientation
questions: Is this Platonism you already had in the Cave, or a new use of it?
How would Mill’s competent judges sit with ‘unselfing’?

the picture of a naked will issuing choices (existentialist/Kantian thinness) misses moral life as vision and attention
